Here we define the linear code we will be using in later construction (a
generalization of the so-called Reed-Solomon code, see~\cite{Blahut83}).
In its application in our paper only its basic quantitative
properties are used, so the details can safely be skipped at first reading.

Let our codewords (information symbols and check symbols together) be
binary strings of length \( N l \)\gloprocn:cap@\( N \).)))\gloprocl@\( l \).))) for some \( l \),
\( N \).
The \emph{symbols} of our codewords, 
binary strings of length \( l \), will be interpreted as elements of the
finite field \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \)\index{Galois field}\gloprocgf@\( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \).))) and
thus, each binary string \( c \) of length \( N l \) will be treated as a vector
\( \mathopen( c(0),\dots,c(N - 1)\mathclose) \) over \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \).
(Note that the word ``field'' is used in two different senses in the
present paper.)
Let us fix \( N \) distinct nonzero elements
\( \alpha_{i} \)\gloproca.greek@\( \alpha_{i} \).))) of \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \) and let \( t < N/2 \) be a
positive integer.
The codewords are those vectors \( c \) that satisfy the equations
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:RS-code}
  \sum_{i = 0}^{N - 1}\alpha_{i}^{j}c(i).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}^{k} = 0\ (j = 1,\dots, 2t)
 \end{equation}
where the addition, multiplication and taking to power \( j \) are
performed in the field \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \).
These are \( 2t \) linear equations.
If we fix the first \( N - 2t \) elements of the vector in any way, (these
are the \emph{information symbols}) the remaining \( 2t \) elements (the \emph{error check
symbols}) can be chosen in a way to satisfy the equations.
This set of equations is always solvable, since its determinant is a
Vandermonde determinant.

Below, we will show a procedure for correcting any \( \nu \le t \) nonzero
errors.
This demonstrates that for the correction of error in any \( \le t \) symbols,
only \( 2t \) error-check symbols are needed.
(Robert Solovay noticed that in our applications,
with a little deterioration of efficiency, even the most brute-force
decoding algorithm is sufficient.
We will never have to correct more than some constant number \( c \) of errors,
so the complexity of decoding would never go much over \( n^{c} \) steps.)

If \( E =\mathopen( e_{0},\dots, e_{N - 1}\mathclose) \) is the sequence of errors then \( C + E \)
will be the observed the word.
Only \( e_{i_{r }} \) are nonzero for \( r =1,\dots,\nu \).
Let \( Y_{r }=e_{i_{r }}, X_{r }=\alpha_{i_{r }} \).
We define the \emph{syndrome} \( S_{j} \) for \( j=1,\dots,2t \) by
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:S_{j}}
	S_{j} = \sum_{i} (c_{i}+e_{i})\alpha_{i}^{j}
		= \sum_{i} e_{i}\alpha_{i}^{j} 	
	   	= \sum_{r } Y_{r } X_{r }^{j}
 \end{equation}
  which can clearly be computed from the codeword: it is the amount by
which the codeword violates the \( j \)-th error check equation.
We will show, using the last expression, that \( Y_{r } \) and \( X_{r } \) can be
determined using \( S_{j} \).
Define the auxiliary polynomial
 \[
	\Lambda(x)=\prod_{r }(1-xX_{r })=\sum_{s=0}^{\nu} \Lambda_{s} x^{s}
 \]
 whose roots are \( X_{r }^{-1} \).
Let us show how to find the coefficients \( \Lambda_{s} \) for \( s>0 \).
We have, for any \( r = 1,\dots, \nu \), and any \( j = 1, \dots, 2t - \nu \):
 \[
	0	= Y_{r }X_{r }^{j+\nu}\Lambda(X_{r }^{-1})		
		= \sum_{s} \Lambda_{s} Y_{r } X_{r }^{j+\nu-s}.     
 \]
  Hence, summing for \( r  \), 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:key}
	0 = \sum_{s = 0}^{\nu} \Lambda_{s}(\sum_{r } Y_{r } X_{r }^{j+\nu-s})
	= \sum_{s = 0}^{\nu} \Lambda_{s} S_{j+\nu-s}\ (j = 1,\dots, 2t - \nu)
 \end{equation}
  hence using \( \Lambda_{0}=1 \),
 \( \sum_{s=1}^{\nu} \Lambda_{s} S_{j+\nu-s}=-S_{j+\nu} \).
This is a system of linear equations for \( \Lambda_{s} \) whose coefficients are
the syndroms, known to us, and whose matrix \( M_{\nu} \) is nonsingular.
Indeed, \( M_{\nu} = ABA^{T} \) where \( B \) is the diagonal matrix
\( {\mathopen\langle Y_{r }X_{r }\mathclose\rangle} \) and \( A \) is the Vandermonde matrix \( A_{j,r }=X^{j-1}_{r } \).

A decoding algorithm now works as follows.
For \( \nu = 1,2,\dots,t \), see if \( M_{\nu} \) is nonsingular, then compute
\( \Lambda(x) \) and find its roots by simple trial-and-error, computing
\( \Lambda(\alpha_{i}^{-1}) \) for all \( i \).
Then, find \( Y_{r } \) by solving the set of equations~\eqref{eq:S_{j}} and
see if the resulting corrected vector \( C \) satisfies~\eqref{eq:RS-code}.
If yes, stop.
(There is also a faster way for determining \( \Lambda(x) \), via the Euclidean
algorithm, see~\cite{Blahut83}).

To make the code completely constructive we must find an effective
representation of the field operations of \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{l}) \).
This finite field can be efficiently represented as the set of remainders
with respect to an irreducible polynomial of degree \( l \) over \( \mathrm{GF}(2) \), so
what is needed is a way to generate large irreducible polynomials.
  Now, it follows from the theory of fields that
 \[
	x^{2\cdot 3^{s}} + x^{3^{s}} +1 
 \]
  is irreducible over \( \mathrm{GF}<(2) \) for any \( s \).
So, the scheme works for all \( l \) of the form \( 2\cdot 3^{s} \).
<!-- end example-11 -->
<!-- example-12: body_md -->
\label{xmp:no-stretch}
Let us use the notation of Proposition~\ref{propo:fitted} with \( a_{k}=1 \) for all \( k \).
Our goal is to give more details of state spaces \( {\mathbb{S}}_{k} \) and
codes \( \varphi_{k} \) satisfying the conditions of that Proposition.
 See Figure~\ref{fig:no-stretch}.
 The error check symbols for \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \) are on a track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Redun\/}}}}^{k} \).
 As the address \( a_{k}=1 \) is controlled by \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k} \),  the cell with address 1
 is not used for error checks.
 The other parts of the information needed to represent the big cell are
 on track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{L\/}}}}^{k} \).
It contains in its different segments the fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{L\/}}}}^{k+1} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Redun\/}}}}^{k+1} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Work\/}}}}^{k+1} \)
of the big cell represented by the colony, as well as its own error check symbols.
There is also a collection of tracks shown here as a single track
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Work\/}}}}^{k} \): it contains for example \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}^{k} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}^{k} \).
<!-- end example-12 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{propo:small-bandwidth}
  In a hierarchical code \( (\varphi_{k}) \) 
  let \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{H\/}}}}_{k} \) denote any track of \( M_{k} \) that is not needed to restore information
  in a cell of \( M_{k+1} \) from the colony coding it.
  (It may contain error-checks or other administrative information like addresses.)
  Then \( \sum_{k} |\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{H\/}}}}_{k}|/\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Cap\/}}}_{k} < 1 \).
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let \( h_{k}=|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{H\/}}}}_{k}|/\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Cap\/}}}_{k} \), \( r_{k}=1-h_{k} \).
  The state of a cell of \( M_{k+1} \) must be represented by the
colony even when we exclude the track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{H\/}}}}_{k} \), so
 \begin{align*}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Cap\/}}}_{k+1}(r_{k+1}+ h_{k+1}) &\le  {Q}_{k}\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Cap\/}}}_{k} r_{k} = \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Cap\/}}}_{k+1}r_{k},
\\    r_{k+1} + h_{k+1} &\le  r_{k},
\\    h_{k+1} &\le  r_{k} - r_{k+1},
 \end{align*}
 allowing to estimate \( \sum_{k}h_{k} \) by a telescoping sum.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- notation-3: body_md -->
Let \( {\Lambda}(n) \)\gloprocl.cap.s@\( {\Lambda}(n) \).)))
 be an increasing sequence of finite subsets of \( {\Lambda} \) with
\( \bigcup_{n}{\Lambda}(n)={\Lambda} \), for example
 \[
   {\Lambda}(n)=([-n,n]\cap \mathbb{Z})^{d}
 \] 
if \( {\Lambda}=\mathbb{Z}^{d} \).
We can view an element \( {\mathbf{s}} \) of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{{\Lambda}(n)} \) as a vector whose
components are indexed with the elements of \( {\Lambda}(n) \).
For a measure \( \nu \) over configurations, denote 
 \gloprocn:greek@\( \nu({\mathbf{s}}) \).))) 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:nu(s)}
  \nu({\mathbf{s}})= \nu\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\xi : \xi(x) = s_{x}\text{ for all }x\in{\Lambda}(n)\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
 \end{equation}
For \( n=0 \), we have the special case
 \( \nu(s)=\nu\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\xi : \xi(0)=s\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} \).

If \( (\mu,\eta) \) is a random trajectory of a probabilistic cellular
automaton then let \( \mu^{t} \)\gloprocm.greek@\( \mu^{t} \).))) be the distribution of the
configuration \( \eta(\cdot,t) \).
<!-- end notation-3 -->
<!-- definition-51: body_md -->
\label{def:weak-conv}
A sequence \( \nu_{k} \) of measures over \( {\mathbb{S}}^{{\Lambda}} \)
 \emph{weakly converges}\index{weak convergence} to measure \( \nu \) if 
\( \lim_{k}\nu_{k}({\mathbf{s}})=\nu({\mathbf{s}}) \) for
all \( n \) and for all \( {\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbb{S}}^{{\Lambda}(n)} \).
<!-- end definition-51 -->
<!-- definition-52: body_md -->
Assuming for simplicity, \( {\Lambda}=\mathbb{Z} \),
we define the \emph{Markov operator}\index{Markov!operator}
\( P \) on measures by
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:P.def}
  (P\mu)({\mathbf{s}})= \sum_{\mathbf{r}}
  \prod_{j=-n+1}^{n-1} \mathbf{P}(s_{j},(r_{j-1},r_{j},r_{j+1})) \mu({\mathbf{r}})
 \end{equation}
 where the summation goes over all possible strings
 \( \mathbf{r}=(r_{-n},\dots,r_{n})\in{\mathbb{S}}^{2n+1} \).
Given a Markov operator, we call a measure \( \alpha \) over configurations
\emph{invariant}\index{measure!invariant} if \( P\alpha=\alpha \).
<!-- end definition-52 -->
<!-- definition-53: body_md -->
A probabilistic cellular automaton is called \emph{ergodic}\index{ergodic}
  if
  \begin{alphenum}
  \item\label{i:ergodic.a} It has only one invariant measure \( \nu \).
  \item\label{i:ergodic.b}
    For every possible measure \( \mu^{0} \) over configurations, \( \mu^{t}=P^{t} \mu^{0} \)
    converges weakly to \( \nu \).
  \end{alphenum}
<!-- end definition-53 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
No examples are known of noisy cellular automata over an infinite space
  that satisfy~\ref{i:ergodic.a} but not~\ref{i:ergodic.b}.
  In one dimension and continuous time there is no such example, as shown in~\cite{Mountford95}.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-54: body_md -->
A deterministic cellular automaton
\( R \)\gloprocrem:cap@\( R \).)))\index{Toom rule} given by Toom can be defined as follows.
We start from a two-dimensional deterministic cellular automaton \( R \)
with set of states \( \{0,1\} \), by the neighborhood \( H= \)
\( \mathopen\{(0,0),(0,1),(1,0)\mathclose\} \).
The transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_R(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}) \) is the majority of
\( x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} \).
<!-- end definition-54 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The notion of ergodicity was defined only for trajectories of \( R_{\varepsilon} \)
that are also trajectories of some probabilistic cellular automaton \( R' \)
(as defined in Section~\ref{sec:PCA}) such that \( R'\subseteq R_{\varepsilon} \),
that is that all trajectories of \( R' \) are trajectories of \( R_{\varepsilon} \).
The difference between \( R_{\varepsilon} \) and \( R' \) is that the local
transition probabilities of a trajectory of \( R' \) are fixed and the
same everywhere in space-time, while \( R_{\varepsilon} \) requires them
only to be within some range.
Toom's theorem implies that no such \( R' \) is ergodic.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- definition-55: body_md -->
Let us define the variation distance for measures \( \mu \) and \( \nu \)
are restricted to \( {\mathbb{S}}^{{\Lambda}(n)} \): 
 \gloprocd@\( d^{n}(\mu, \nu) \).))) 
 \[
 d^{n}(\mu,\nu) 
= \sum\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu|\mu({\mathbf{s}})-\nu({\mathbf{s}})|\text{ for all } {\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbb{S}}^{{\Lambda}(n)}\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
 \]
<!-- end definition-55 -->
<!-- definition-56: body_md -->
For the set of sites 
 \gloprocc.cap@\( {\Lambda}_{m} \).))) 
 \[
 {\Lambda}_{m}=\mathbb{Z}_{m}\times\mathbb{Z}_{m}
 \]
  where \( m \) can be finite or infinite, suppose that the local transition matrix (for
simplicity, with nearest-neighbor interaction) gives rise to an
ergodic Markov process with Markov operator \( P_{m} \)\gloprocp.cap@\( P_{m} \).))).
Let 
 \gloprocdef:cap@\( D^{n}_{m}(t) \).)))
 \[
 D^{n}_{m}(t) = \bigvee_{\mu,\nu} d^{n}(P_{m}^{t}\mu, P_{m}^{t}\nu),
\]
where the dependence on the transition matrix is understood but is not shown.
<!-- end definition-56 -->
<!-- definition-57: body_md -->
\label{def:relaxation-time}
We will call the function 
 \gloprocr@\( r_{m}(n,\delta) \).))) 
 \[
  r_{m}(n,\delta) := \sup\mathopen\{\verythinmathskipt : D^{n}_{m}(t)>\delta\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}<\infty
 \]
 the \emph{relaxation time}\index{relaxation time}.
<!-- end definition-57 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:unif}
  For all \( n<(m-1)/2 \), for all \( \delta \) with \( r_{\infty}(n,\delta)<(m-1)/2-n \)
we have
  \[
   r_{m}(n,\delta)\le r_{\infty}(n,\delta).
  \]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Take \( m,n,\delta \) satisfying the above conditions and let
\( r=r_{\infty}(n,\delta) \).
  Due to the monotonicity of \( D^{n}_{m}(t) \), it is enough to prove that 
\( D^{n}_{m}(r)\le D^{n}_{\infty}(r) \).
Take a measure \( \nu \) over configurations of \( {\Lambda}_{m} \), this will give
rise to some measure \( \nu_{\infty} \) over configurations of period \( m \) in
\( {\Lambda}_{\infty} \) in a natural way, where \( \nu_{\infty} \) is such that for all
\( n<(m-1)/2 \) and all \( {\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbb{S}}^{{\Lambda}(n)} \) 
we have \( \nu_{\infty}({\mathbf{s}})=\nu({\mathbf{s}}) \).
Then, \( r<(m-1)/2-n \) implies \( 2n+1+2r<m \) and therefore via~\eqref{eq:P.def}
we have
 \[
  P_{m}^r\nu({\mathbf{s}})=P_{\infty}^r\nu_{\infty}({\mathbf{s}}).
 \]
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- example-13: body_md -->
Let \( \xi_{0} \) be the configuration over the one-dimensional integer
lattice that is 0 in the even places and 1 in odd places, and \( \xi_{1} \)
the one that is 1 in the even places and 0 in the odd places.
For \( b=0,1 \) let \( \mu_{b} \) be the measure concentrated on \( \xi_{b} \),
and let \( P \) be the linear operator obtained from some transition function.
Suppose that the measures \( P^{n}\mu_{0} \) converge to some measure
\( \nu_{0} \).
Then the measures \( P^{n}\mu_{1} \) converge to some measure \( \nu_{1} \).
Even if \( \nu_{1} \) is different from \( \nu_{0} \) they differ only by a
translation in space.
If the translations of \( \nu_{0} \) are the only invariant measures of
\( P \) then we would still say that in some sense, \( P \) loses all
information about the initial configuration: we might say, it loses
all ``local'' information.
Indeed, a cell has no way of knowing whether it has even or odd
coordinates.
<!-- end example-13 -->
<!-- definition-58: body_md -->
We can call the Markov operator \( P \)
 \emph{strongly not forgetful}\index{forgetful!strongly not} if it has two
disjoint (weakly) closed translation-invariant sets of measures.
<!-- end definition-58 -->
<!-- definition-59: body_md -->
Let us be given an arbitrary one-dimensional transition function
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) and the integers \( N,L \).
We define the three-dimensional transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \) as follows.
  The interaction neighborhood is \( H\times\{-1,0,1\} \) with the
neighborhood \( H \) defined in Section~\ref{sec:toom} above.
  The transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \) says: in order to obtain your state at
time \( t+1 \), first apply the transition function \( R \) in each plane defined by
fixing the third coordinate.
  Then, apply transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) on each line obtained by fixing
the first and second coordinates.
\footnote{The papers~\cite{GacsReif3dim88} and \cite{Gacs2dim89} use a
neighborhood instead of \( H \) that makes some proofs easier: the
northern, south-eastern and south-western neighbors.}

For an integer \( m \), define the space \( {\Lambda} =\mathbb{Z}_{m}^{2}\times \mathbb{Z}_{N} \).
For a trajectory \( \xi \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}) \) on \( \mathbb{Z}_{N} \), define the
trajectory \( \zeta \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}') \) on \( {\Lambda} \) by
 \begin{equation} \label{eq:reifCode} 
	\zeta(i,j,n,t)=\xi(n,t).
 \end{equation} 
  Thus, each cell of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}) \) is repeated \( m^{2} \) times, on a whole
``plane'' (a torus for finite \( m \)) in \( {\Lambda} \).
<!-- end definition-59 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
There are constants
\( \varepsilon_{0},c_{1},d_{1}>0 \) such that the following holds.
For all \( N,L \), and \( m=c_{1} \log(N L) \), for any trajectory \( \xi \) of
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}) \) over \( \mathbb{Z}_{N} \), if the trajectory \( \zeta \) of
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}') \) is defined by~\eqref{eq:reifCode} then for any
\( \varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0} \), any trajectory \( (\mu,\eta) \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}_{\varepsilon}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}') \)
such that \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\zeta(\cdot,0) \) we have for all \( t \) in
\( (0,L] \) and all \( w\in {\Lambda} \)
 \[ 
  \mu\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\eta(w,t)\ne  \zeta(w,t)\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} \le d_{1}\varepsilon .
 \]
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:1dim.comp.finite}
  Let \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) be a standard computing transition function over an alphabet \( \Sigma \),
  and \( \delta>0 \) a constant.
  There is
 \begin{itemize}
  \item a transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \) with a state space \( {\mathbb{S}} \) having fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \),
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \);
\item a code \( \psi_{*}: \Sigma_{0}^{*}\to {\mathbb{S}}^{*} \) with \( |\psi_{*}(\rho)|\le 2|\rho| \),
  \item constants \( c_{1}, c_{2}>1 \)
 \end{itemize}
 such that the following holds for all sufficiently small \( \varepsilon \).
 Let \( N \) be the size of our space, and \( \rho\in\Sigma_{0}^{*} \) with
 \( 2|\rho|<N \), \( \varepsilon<\varepsilon_{0} \).
 Let \( \zeta(x,t) \) be any trajectory of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) with
 \( \zeta(x,0).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}}=\rho(x) \) for \( x\in\left[0,|\rho|\right) \) and filled with \( * \)'s
 otherwise.
 Let \( \eta \) be any trajectory over the space \( \mathbb{Z}^{N} \)
 of an \( \varepsilon \)-perturbation of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \), with
 \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Init\/}}}_{\psi_{*}}(\rho) \).
 For all sufficiently small \( \varepsilon \), for all
 \( t \) for which \( \zeta(\cdot,t) \) does not use more space than \( N \),
all \( t'>t\cdot h_{1}(t,c_{1}) \), all \( x\in\mathbb{Z} \) we have
 \[
 \operatorname{\mathsf P}\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\zeta(x, t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \not\preceq \eta(x, t').\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}}\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} < \delta + t'\varepsilon^{h_{0}(N,c_{2})}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- example-14: body_md -->
Let $V=(a_{1},a_{2}]\times(t,u]$, ${B}  < d = 0.2 (a_{2}-a_{1})$.
Suppose that we are given some ${\mathbf{r}}\in{\mathbb{S}}^{3}$, $s\in{\mathbb{S}}$.
Let ${g}(\eta)=1$ if there is a space-time point $(x,t_{0})$ in $V$, and an
$\varepsilon<d$ such that $\eta(x+i{B} ,t)=r_{i}$ for $i = -1, 0, 1$ during
the interval $\left[t_{0}-\varepsilon,t_{0}\right)$ and $\eta(x,t_{0})=s$.
Thus, the event ${g}(\eta)=1$ marks a certain kind of transition in the window.
<!-- end example-14 -->
<!-- definition-60: body_md -->
\label{def:traj}
  A random history $\eta$ will be called a
\emph{trajectory}\index{trajectory!weak} of medium $M$ given in~\eqref{eq:med}
if for each time $u\ge 0$, for each set of disjoint local conditions
 \[
  (\alpha_{i},V_{i})_{i\le N}
 \]
  with $(\cmforall{i})\inf\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{t}} V_{i}\ge u$ (where $\inf\emptyset=\infty$), 
we have
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:weak-traj-def}
   \operatorname{\mathsf{E}}{\Bigl[ \prod_{i}{g}(\alpha_{i}, V_{i},\eta)\Bigm\vert \mathcal{A}_{<u}\Bigr]}
   \le \prod_{i} b(\alpha_{i}).
 \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-60 -->
<!-- example-15: body_md -->
\label{xmp:PCA-medium}
\begin{sloppypar}
 Let us be given a probabilistic cellular automaton
$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P},{B} ,{T} )$.
For each state vector ${\mathbf{r}}\in {\mathbb{S}}^{3}$ and state $s$, let us form type
$\alpha(s,{\mathbf{r}})$.                               
The condition of this type will say that the transition rules are obeyed at times
of the form $n{T} $.
Namely for cell $x$, time $t$ of the form $n{T} $ with $n>0$, let 
\end{sloppypar}
 \begin{align}\label{eq:PCA-medium}
\nonumber      {g}\bigl(\alpha(s,{\mathbf{r}}),\;\{x\} &\times(t-{T} ,t],\;\eta\bigr)
\\        &= \{ \eta(x+i{B} ,t-{T} /2)=r_{i}\;(i=-1,0,1),\;\eta(x,t)=s \},
\\    b(\alpha(s,r)) &= \mathbf{P}(s,{\mathbf{r}}).
 \end{align}
  For all cells $x$ and rational times $u$ we define a new type
 $\beta=\beta(x,u)$                        
 by $b(\beta(x,u)) = 0$ and
 \[
  {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\beta(x,u),\;\{x\}\times[{T} {\lfloor u/{T} \rfloor},u],\;\eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
   = \mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\eta(x,u)\ne\eta(x,{T} {\lfloor u/{T} \rfloor})\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
 \]
This condition says that $\eta(x,u)=\eta(x,{T} {\lfloor u/{T} \rfloor})$ with probability 1.
For all other combinations $\alpha,V$ we set ${g}(\alpha,V,\eta)=0$.
It is easy to see that the trajectories of $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P},{B} ,{T} )$ are
trajectories of the medium defined this way.
<!-- end example-15 -->
<!-- definition-61: body_md -->
\label{def:state-subsets}
In a probabilistic cellular automaton $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P},{B} ,{T} )$ 
for each set of states $E$ and state vector ${\mathbf{r}}=(r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1})$ let
\( \mathbf{P}(E,{\mathbf{r}})=\sum_{q\in E}\mathbf{P}(q,{\mathbf{r}}) \).
Let $\mathbf{K}$\gloprock.cap@$\mathbf{K}$.))) be the set of functions $K:{\mathbb{S}}^{3}\to 2^{{\mathbb{S}}}$
such that
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:K-def}
  K({\mathbf{r}})\subseteq \mathopen\{\verythinmathskips\ne r_{0}: \mathbf{P}(s,{\mathbf{r}})>0\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}.
  \end{equation}
  For a space-time trajectory \( \eta \) and a \( K\in\mathbf{K} \) let us write 
 \gloprock.cap@\( \overline{K}(x,t,\eta) \).))) 
 \[
   \overline{K}(x,t,\eta)=K(\eta(x-{B} ,t), \eta(x,t), \eta(x+{B} ,t)).
 \]
  For all \( K',K''\in\mathbf{K} \) with \( K'\supseteq K'' \) (that is \( K'({\mathbf{r}})\supseteq K''({\mathbf{r}}) \)
  for all \( {\mathbf{r}} \)), let 
 \gloprocc.cap@\( c(K',K'') \).))) 
 \[
   c(K',K'') =\bigvee_{{\mathbf{r}}} \frac{\mathbf{P}(K''({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}})}{\mathbf{P}(K'({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}})}
 \]
  be the maximum conditional probability, over all \( {\mathbf{r}} \), of
getting into the set \( K''({\mathbf{r}}) \) provided we get into the set \( K'({\mathbf{r}}) \).  

In case of a continuous-time cellular automaton \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}}(\mathbf{R},{B} ) \),
for any functions \( K,K',K''\in\mathbf{K} \) with \( \mathbf{R}(K,{\mathbf{r}}) = \sum_{q\in K}\mathbf{R}(q,{\mathbf{r}}) \)
we define the corresponding quantity \gloprocc@\( c(K',K'') \).)))  
 \begin{align*}
c(K',K'')   = \bigvee_{{\mathbf{r}}}\frac{\mathbf{R}(K''({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}})}{\mathbf{R}(K'({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}})}.
 \end{align*}
<!-- end definition-61 -->
<!-- example-16: body_md -->
\label{xmp:PCA-stop}
In case of a probabilistic cellular automaton \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P},{B} ,{T} ) \),
for each pair of such functions \( K',K''\in \mathbf{K} \) with \( K'\supseteq K'' \) let us form the type 
 \gloproca.greek@\( \alpha(K',K'') \).)))
 \[
  \alpha =\alpha(K', K'').
 \]
  For each cell \( x \) and times \( u\le v \) of the form \( n{T}  \), let us form the 
rectangle \( V=\{x\}\times(u,v] \).
  For each such pair \( \alpha,V \) let 
  \( {g}(\alpha,V,\eta)=1 \) if there is a first \( t\in(u,v] \) with
 \( \eta(x,t)\in \overline{K}'(x,t-{T} ,\eta) \) and in it, we have
 \( \eta(x,t)\in \overline{K}''(x,t-{T} ,\eta) \).
 Also, let \( b(\alpha)=c(K',K'') \).
 The condition of type \( \alpha \) bounds the probability that as soon as
 we get into the set \( K' \) we also get into the set \( K'' \).
<!-- end example-16 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{propo:discr-stop}
  If \( M \) is the medium defined by the conditions above then all trajectories of 
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P}, {B} , {T} ) \) are trajectories of  \( M \).
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- example-17: body_md -->
\label{xmp:CCA-stop}
In case of a continuous-time cellular automaton \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}}(\mathbf{R},{B} ) \)
we define each \( \alpha(K',K'') \), \( V=\{x\}\times(u,v] \) and \( {g}(\alpha,V,\eta) \)
as in Example~\ref{xmp:PCA-stop}, but now for all rational \( u<v \).
<!-- end example-17 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:cont-stop}
  Every trajectory of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}}(\mathbf{R},{B} ) \) is a trajectory of the medium defined
in the above example.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
As in the time-discretization in
Section~\ref{sec:Markov}, for a small \( \delta>0 \), let
\( M_{\delta}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P},{B} ,\delta) \) with \( \mathbf{P}(s,{\mathbf{r}})=\delta\mathbf{R}(s,{\mathbf{r}}) \) when
 \( s\ne r_{0} \) and \( 1-\delta\sum_{s'\ne r_{0}}\mathbf{R}(s',{\mathbf{r}}) \) otherwise.
  Then a transition to the limit \( \delta\to 0 \) in
Proposition~\ref{propo:discr-stop} completes the proof. 
  The transition uses the fact that trajectories of \( M(\delta) \) converge in
distribution to trajectories of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}}(\mathbf{R},{B} ) \).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-62: body_md -->
\label{def:stopping-time}
A real random variable $\sigma$ with values in $\left[0,\infty\right)$ is a
\emph{stopping time}\index{stopping time} if for each $t$
the event $\{\sigma\le t\}$ is in $\mathcal{A}_{t}$.
Let $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}$\gloproca.cap@$\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}$.))) be the algebra of events $A$ with
the property that $A\cap\{\sigma\le t\}\in \mathcal{A}_{t}$.
<!-- end definition-62 -->
<!-- definition-63: body_md -->
For some time interval $J\subset(0,\infty]$, assume that there
  is a stopping time \( \sigma\in J \), and random variables \( \alpha(\eta)\in\mathbb{T} \), 
  $V(\eta)\in\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Rectangles\/}}}$ \gloprocv.cap@$V^{t}(\eta)$.)))
  measurable in $\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}$, with
 \[
  \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{t}} V^{\sigma}(\eta)\subseteq J\cap[\sigma,\infty].
 \]
The tuple \( (J,\sigma,\alpha(\eta),V(\eta)) \) will be called a
\emph{constraint process}\index{constraint process}.
<!-- end definition-63 -->
<!-- definition-64: body_md -->
A random history $\eta$ will be called a
\emph{strong trajectory}\index{trajectory} if for each system of disjoint
constraint processes 
\begin{align*}
   (J,\sigma_{i},\alpha_{i}(\eta), V_{i}(\eta))_{i\in N}
\end{align*}
(where \( V_{i}(\eta) \) are disjoint for each \( \eta \)),
$h$ an event function over $\mathcal{A}_{<\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{t}} J}$, we have
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:traj-def}
   \operatorname{\mathsf{E}}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu h
     \prod_{i}{g}(\alpha_{i}(\eta),V_{i}(\eta),\eta)\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
   \le \operatorname{\mathsf{E}} h\operatorname{\mathsf{E}}\prod_{i} b(\alpha_{i}(\eta)).
 \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-64 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
The trajectories of the cellular automaton \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbb{P},{B}, {T}) \) of
  Example~\ref{xmp:PCA-stop} are strong.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The statement follows by a standard argument from the strong Markov
property of the Markov process \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{B}, {B} , {T} ) \) (see~\cite{Neveu64}).
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{propo:discr-stop} and Theorem~\ref{thm:cont-stop}
  can be strengthened: all trajectories of 
  \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{B}, {B} , {T} ) \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}}(\mathbf{R},{B}) \)  are \emph{strong} trajectories of
  the corresponding media.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- definition-65: body_md -->
\label{def:canon-simul}
  Let \( M, M^{*} \) be media where the functions \( g,b \) define the constraints on \( M \),
  and \( g^{*},b^{*} \) define those for \( M^{*} \),
  and let \( \varphi^{*} \) be a mapping from the
histories of \( M \) into those of \( M^{*} \): we
will write \( \eta^{*}=\varphi^{*}(\eta) \).
We say that \( \varphi^{*} \) is a \emph{canonical simulation map}
\index{simulation!canonical}
if the following holds.
Let \( (\alpha,V) \) be any local condition for \( M^{*} \) with
\( \alpha\in\mathbb{T}^{*} \).
Then there is a system of constraint processes
\gloprocbaij@\( \beta_{i,j}(\alpha) \).))) 
\gloprocwtaijve@\( W^{t}_{i,j}(\eta) \).))) 
\gloproctaijve@\( \tau_{i,j} \).))) 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:weak-canonical-sys}
   {\bigl(\mskip 1mu\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{t}} V, \tau_{i,j},\beta_{i,j}(\eta), W_{i,j}(\eta)\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \end{equation}
 with \( i=1,\dots,n(\alpha,V) \), \( j=1,\dots,k(\alpha,V,i) \)
 with the following properties.
 For each fixed \( i \), the subsystem containing elements for that
\( i \) forms a system of disjoint constraint processes with
\( W_{i,j}(\eta)\subseteq V \), and for almost all \( \eta \) we have
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:canonical}
 \begin{aligned}
   {g}^{*}(\alpha,V,\eta^{*}) &
    \le \sum_{i}\prod_{j}{g}(\beta_{i,j}(\eta), W_{i,j}(\eta),\eta),
\\ b^{*}(\alpha) &\ge \sum_{i}\prod_{j} b(\beta_{i,j}(\eta)).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-65 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:canonical}
                                              
  If \( \varphi^{*} \) is a canonical simulation map then for each
strong trajectory \( \eta \) of \( M \), the expression \( \varphi^{*}(\eta) \) defines
a strong trajectory of \( M^{*} \).
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
et \( \eta \) be a strong trajectory of \( M \) and
  \begin{align}\label{eq:the-constr-proc}
 (J, \sigma_{l}, \alpha_{l}(\eta^{*}),V_{l}(\eta^{*}))_{l\in N}  
\end{align}
  a system of disjoint random local conditions in \( M^{*} \).
Let \( h \) be an event function measurable in \( \mathcal{A}_{<\inf J} \).
We must show
 \[
 \operatorname{\mathsf{E}} {\bigl(\verythinmathskiph\prod_{l}{g}^{*}_{l}(\alpha_{l}(\eta^{*}),V_{l}(\eta^{*}),\eta^{*})\mskip 1mu\bigr)} 
  \le \operatorname{\mathsf{E}} h \operatorname{\mathsf{E}}\prod_{l} b^{*}(\alpha^{\sigma_{l}}_{l}(\eta^{*})).
 \]
  By the assumption, for each value \( (a,v) \) of the random
  \( (\alpha_{l}(\eta^{*}), V_{l}(\eta^{*})) \)
  there is a system of constraint processes
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:W-sys}
 {\bigl(\mskip 1mu\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{t}} v,\tau_{l,i,j}(a,v),\beta_{l,i,j}(a,v,\eta), W_{l,i,j}(a,v,\eta)\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \end{equation}
  for \( i=1,\dots,n(a,v) \), \( j=1,\dots,k(a,v,i) \), with the
  properties defined for canonical simulations, so \( \tau_{l.i,j}\in\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\text{t}} v \).
  This implies
  \begin{align}\label{eq:tau-sigma}
   \tau_{l,i,j}(\alpha_{l}(\eta^{*}),V_{l}(\eta^{*}))\ge\sigma_{l}
  \end{align}
  for all \( l,i,j \).
  We will use the shorthand notation
\begin{align}\label{eq:bar-notation}
   \bar W_{l,i,j}(\eta)=W_{l,i,j}(\alpha_{l}(\eta^{*}),V_{l}(\eta^{*}),\eta),
\end{align}
and \( \bar\tau_{l,i,j} \), \( \bar \beta_{l,i,j}(\eta) \) means similarly not showing the
dependence on \( \alpha_{l},V_{l} \).
  
  \begin{claimnonumber}
    For each \( l,i,j \), the tuple
   \begin{align*}
 (J,\bar\tau_{l,i,j},\bar\beta_{l,i,j}(\eta), \bar W_{l,i,j}(\eta))  
\end{align*}
is a constraint process.
  \end{claimnonumber}
 \begin{proof}
   Let us first show that \( \bar\tau_{l,i,j} \) is a stopping time.
   Let
\begin{align*}
   E_{a,v}\mathrel{\;\Leftrightarrow\;} (\alpha_{l}(\eta^{*}),V_{l}(\eta^{*}))=(a,v).
\end{align*}
We have
   \begin{align}\label{eq:tau-union}
     \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t \mathrel{\;\Leftrightarrow\;} \bigvee_{a,v}\tau_{l,i,j}(a,v)\le t\land E_{a,v}.
   \end{align}
From~\eqref{eq:tau-sigma} we get that
\( \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t \) implies \( \sigma_{l}\le t \), therefore 
\begin{align*}
\bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t\land E_{a,v}\mathrel{\;\Leftrightarrow\;} \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t\land\sigma_{l}\le t\land E_{a,v}.
\end{align*}
   By the definition of stopping times, \( \{\tau_{l,i,j}(a,v)\le t\}\in\mathcal{A}_{t} \).
   Because~\eqref{eq:the-constr-proc} is a constraint process for each \( l \),
we have also 
\begin{align}\label{eq:E_{a,v}}
 \{\sigma_{l}\le t\land E_{a,v}\}\in\mathcal{A}_{t},
\end{align}
hence the countable union~\eqref{eq:tau-union} is also in \( \mathcal{A}_{t} \).
Similarly, for all \( (b, w)\in \mathbb{T}\times\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Rectangles\/}}} \), the event  
   \begin{align}\label{eq:W-event}
  \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t \land (\bar\beta_{l,i,j}(\eta),\bar W_{l,i,j}(\eta))=(b,w)
   \end{align}
   can be written as
\begin{align*}
  \bigvee_{a,v}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\sigma_{l}\le t \land E_{a,v}\land \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t
  \land (\beta_{l,i,j}(a,v,\eta),W_{l,i,j}(a,v,\eta))=(b,w)\mskip 1mu\bigr)}.
\end{align*}
We have seen~\eqref{eq:E_{a,v}}, and because~\eqref{eq:W-sys} is a system of constraint
processes, also 
\begin{align*}
 \{\bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t\land (\beta(a,v,\eta),W_{l,i,j}(a,v,\eta))=(b,w)\}\in\mathcal{A}_{t} ,
\end{align*}
therefore~\eqref{eq:W-event} is in \( \mathcal{A}_{t} \).
 \end{proof}

  By~\eqref{eq:canonical} we have, with \( \bar\alpha_{l}=\alpha_{l}(\eta*) \),
 \( \bar V_{l}=V_{l}(\eta^{*}) \) and the notation in~\eqref{eq:bar-notation}
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:weak-canonical-appl}
 {g}^{*}(\bar\alpha_{l},\bar V_{l},\eta^{*}) \le
   \sum_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=1}^{k} {g}(\bar\beta_{l,i,j}(\eta),\eta),\bar W_{l,i,j}(\eta),\eta).
\end{equation}
Here we did not make \( n \) dependent on \( \bar\alpha_{l} \), \( \bar V_{l} \),
nor \( k \) dependent on these and \( i \),
setting them to the maxima of all the possible values.
Recall the special types \( \omega \), \( \delta \) defined in~\eqref{eq:omega-delta}.
Whenever \( i>n(\bar\alpha_{l},\bar V_{l}) \), we set
\( \beta_{l,i,j}=\omega \), meaning that the \( i \)th additive term is omitted.
And whenever \( j>k(\bar\alpha_{l},\bar V_{l},i) \), we set
\( \beta_{l,i,j}=\delta \), meaning that the \( j \)th multiplicative factor is omitted.
Now
 \[
  \prod_{l} b^{*}(\bar\alpha_{l})\ge
     \prod_{l}\sum_{i}\prod_{j}b(\bar\beta_{l,i,j}(\eta))
 = \sum_{i(\cdot)}\prod_{l,j} b(\bar\beta_{l,i(l),j}(\eta))
 \]
 where the last sum is over all functions \( i(\cdot) \) with \( i(l)\in[1,n] \).
  Similarly, by~\eqref{eq:weak-canonical-appl}
 \[
 {g}^{*}(\bar\alpha_{l},\bar V_{l},\eta^{*}) \le 
   \sum_{i(\cdot)}\prod_{l,j}{g}(\bar\beta_{l,i,j}(\eta),\bar W_{l,i,j}(\eta),\eta).
 \]
  Therefore it is sufficient to show for a fixed function \( i(\cdot) \),
 \[
  \operatorname{\mathsf{E}} {\bigl(\verythinmathskiph\prod_{l,j} g(\bar\beta_{l,i(l),j}(\eta),\bar W_{l,i(l),j}(\eta),\eta)\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
	\le \operatorname{\mathsf{E}} h\operatorname{\mathsf{E}}\prod_{l,j} b(\bar\beta_{l,i(l),j}(\eta)).
 \]
 For any \( l,i \), the rectangles \( \bar W_{l,i,j}(\eta) \) defined in~\eqref{eq:bar-notation}
 are all disjoint, and belong to \( V_{l}(\eta^{*}) \).
  Also the sets \( V_{l}(\eta^{*}) \) are disjoint, therefore all rectangles
 \( \bar W_{l,i(l),j}(\eta) \) are disjoint.
 The Claim has shown that the system
\[
  {\bigl(\verythinmathskipJ,\bar\tau_{l,i(l),j},\bar\beta_{l,i(l),j}(\eta), \bar W_{l,i(l),j}(\eta)\mskip 1mu\bigr)}_{l\in N}
\]
is a system of disjoint constraint processes for \( M \),  and hence the proof is finished by
the strong trajectory property of \( \eta \).
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- claimnonumber-1: body_md -->
For each \( l,i,j \), the tuple
   \begin{align*}
 (J,\bar\tau_{l,i,j},\bar\beta_{l,i,j}(\eta), \bar W_{l,i,j}(\eta))  
\end{align*}
is a constraint process.
<!-- end claimnonumber-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let us first show that \( \bar\tau_{l,i,j} \) is a stopping time.
   Let
\begin{align*}
   E_{a,v}\mathrel{\;\Leftrightarrow\;} (\alpha_{l}(\eta^{*}),V_{l}(\eta^{*}))=(a,v).
\end{align*}
We have
   \begin{align}\label{eq:tau-union}
     \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t \mathrel{\;\Leftrightarrow\;} \bigvee_{a,v}\tau_{l,i,j}(a,v)\le t\land E_{a,v}.
   \end{align}
From~\eqref{eq:tau-sigma} we get that
\( \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t \) implies \( \sigma_{l}\le t \), therefore 
\begin{align*}
\bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t\land E_{a,v}\mathrel{\;\Leftrightarrow\;} \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t\land\sigma_{l}\le t\land E_{a,v}.
\end{align*}
   By the definition of stopping times, \( \{\tau_{l,i,j}(a,v)\le t\}\in\mathcal{A}_{t} \).
   Because~\eqref{eq:the-constr-proc} is a constraint process for each \( l \),
we have also 
\begin{align}\label{eq:E_{a,v}}
 \{\sigma_{l}\le t\land E_{a,v}\}\in\mathcal{A}_{t},
\end{align}
hence the countable union~\eqref{eq:tau-union} is also in \( \mathcal{A}_{t} \).
Similarly, for all \( (b, w)\in \mathbb{T}\times\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Rectangles\/}}} \), the event  
   \begin{align}\label{eq:W-event}
  \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t \land (\bar\beta_{l,i,j}(\eta),\bar W_{l,i,j}(\eta))=(b,w)
   \end{align}
   can be written as
\begin{align*}
  \bigvee_{a,v}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\sigma_{l}\le t \land E_{a,v}\land \bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t
  \land (\beta_{l,i,j}(a,v,\eta),W_{l,i,j}(a,v,\eta))=(b,w)\mskip 1mu\bigr)}.
\end{align*}
We have seen~\eqref{eq:E_{a,v}}, and because~\eqref{eq:W-sys} is a system of constraint
processes, also 
\begin{align*}
 \{\bar\tau_{l,i,j}\le t\land (\beta(a,v,\eta),W_{l,i,j}(a,v,\eta))=(b,w)\}\in\mathcal{A}_{t} ,
\end{align*}
therefore~\eqref{eq:W-event} is in \( \mathcal{A}_{t} \).
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- example-18: body_md -->
Let \( M_{1}\) be the \( \varepsilon \)-perturbation \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}_{\varepsilon}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}},{B}_{1},{T}_{1}) \)
  of the cellular automaton with \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1}=\{0,1\} \) and
the trivial transition function  \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(x,y,z)=0 \) for all \( x,y,z \).
Then \( \eta \) is a trajectory if for \( t>0 \), \( \eta(x,t) \) are 
random variables such that for any \( u \) and any finite set \( S \) of space-time points \( (x,t) \)
with \( t\ge u \), the conditional probability that
\( \eta(x,t)=1 \) in all \( (x,t)\in S \) no matter how the \( \eta(x',t') \) are fixed for all \( t'<t \),
is bounded by \( \varepsilon^{|S|} \).
The set of constraint types consists of a single element, \( \mathbb{T}_{1}=\{\alpha_{1} \} \)
with \( b_{1}(\alpha_{1})=\varepsilon \).
For the event function we have \( g_{1}(\alpha_{1},V,\eta)=1 \) if and only if
for some \( (x,t) \) of the form \( (m{B}_{1}, n{T}_{1}) \) with integers \( m,n \) and \( n>0 \),
\( V=\left[x,x+{B}_{1}\right)\times(t-T_{1},t] \), and \( \eta(x,t)=1 \).

Let  \( M_{2}\)  be  a medium with \( {\mathbb{S}}_{2}=\{0,1\} \).
For integers \( {Q}_{1},{U}_{1}>0 \) let \( {B}_{2}={Q}_{1}{B}_{1} \), \( {T}_{2}={U}_{1}{T}_{1} \).
The histories will be of the form \( \eta(x,t) \) with \( x=m{B}_{2} \), \( t=n{T}_{2} \) for \( n\ge 0 \).
The set of constraint types consists of a single element, \( \mathbb{T}_{2}=\{\alpha_{2} \} \)
with \( b_{2}(\alpha_{2})=3{Q}_{1}{U}_{1}\varepsilon^{2} \).
For the event function we have \( g_{2}(\alpha_{2},V,\eta)=1 \)
if and only if for some \( (x,t) \) of the form \( (n{B}_{1}, n{T}_{1}) \)
with integers \( m,n \) and \( n>0 \),
\( V=\left[x-{B}_{2},x+2{B}_{2}\right)\times(t-2{T}_{2},t] \),
and \( \eta(x,t)=1 \).

Let us define the simulation \( \varphi^{*} \) as follows.
If \( \eta^{*}=\varphi^{*}(\eta) \) then \( \eta^{*}(x,t)=1 \) if and only if
\( (x,t) \) has the form \( (m{B}_{2}, n{T}_{2}) \) with integers \( m,n \) and \( n>0 \),
and in \( V=\left[x-{B}_{2},x+2{B}_{2}\right)\times(t-2{T}_{2},t] \)
there are at least two elements \( (x_{1},t_{1})\ne (x_{2},t_{2}) \)  with \( \eta(x_{i},t_{i})=1 \).
To show that this is a simulation we define the system of local conditions
\[
   {\bigl(\mskip 1mu\beta_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V), W_{i,j}(\alpha,V)\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \]
 as follows.
 These are nonempty if and only if for some \( (x,t) \)
 of the form \( (m{B}_{2}, n{T}_{2}) \) with integer \( m,n \) and \( n>0 \),
 \( V=\left[x-{B}_{2},x+2{B}_{2}\right)\times(t-2{T}_{2},t] \).
 In this case, let \( P=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{N}\} \) be a list of all distinct
 pairs \( \{ (x_{1},t_{1}), (x_{2},t_{2})\} \) in \( V \), where \( N=\binom{6{Q}_{1}{U}_{1}}{2} \).
 For \( p_{i}=\{ (x_{i,1},t_{i,1}), (x_{i,2},t_{i,2})\} \),
 let \( \beta_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V)=\alpha_{1} \) for all \( i,j \),  and 
\begin{align*}
 W_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V)=\left[x_{i,j},x_{i,j}+{B}_{1}\right)\times(t_{i,j}-{T}_{1},{T}_{i,j}].
\end{align*}
Then \( {g}_{2}(\alpha_{2},V,\eta^{*}) \) is the event that 
\( \eta(x,t)=1 \) for at least two pairs \( (x,t)\in V \),
and this is upper-bounded by 
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{i}\prod_{j}g_{1}(\alpha_{1},W_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V))
\end{align*}
as required.
Also 
\begin{align*}
 b_{2}(\alpha_{2})=3{Q}_{1}{U}_{1}\varepsilon^{2}>N\varepsilon^{2}
=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{2}g_{1}(\alpha_{1},W_{i,j}(\alpha_{2},V))
\end{align*}
as required.
<!-- end example-18 -->
<!-- definition-66: body_md -->
\label{def:inj-canon-simul}
  We will call a canonical simulation
\emph{injective}\index{simulation!canonical!injective} if the mapping
\( \varphi^{*} \) is the identity, and the functions
\( b_{2}(\alpha),{g}_{2}(\alpha,\cdot,\cdot) \) differ from \( b_{1},{g}_{1} \) only in
that they are defined for some additional types \( \alpha \), too.
<!-- end definition-66 -->
<!-- definition-67: body_md -->
For some function \( K\in\mathbf{K} \) let 
 \gloproca@\( a_{-1}(K), a_{1}(K) \).))) 
 \begin{alignat*}{3}
        &a_{-1}(K) &&= \bigwedge_{{\mathbf{r}}}\mathbf{R}(K({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}}),
\\   &a_{1}(K)   &&= \bigvee_{{\mathbf{r}}}\mathbf{R}(K({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}}).
 \end{alignat*}
  Let us call a time \( u \) of the history \( \eta \) a
 \emph{\( K \)-switching-time}\index{switch!time} of a cell \( x \) if for all
\( t<u \) sufficiently close to \( u \) we have 
\( \eta(x,t)\notin \overline{K}(x,t,\eta) \) and \( \eta(x,u)\in \overline{K}(x,t,\eta) \), 
that is we have just jumped into the target set determined by \( K(\cdot) \).
For some rational constant \( D>0 \), integers \( k\ge 0 \) and \( j=-1,1 \) let 
 \gloproca.greek@\( \alpha(K,D,k,j) \).))) 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:switch-count}
  {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\alpha(K,D,k,j),\;\{x\}\times(u,u + D],\;\eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \end{equation}
  be the event function of type \( \alpha(K,D,k,j) \) for \( j=-1 \) [\( j=1 \)] for the
event that site \( x \) has at most [at least] \( k \) times during \( (u,u+D] \),
that are \( K \)-switching times.
<!-- end definition-67 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{propo:time-bounds}
Let us define, with \( a_{j}=a_{j}(K) \) and every possible \( h>0 \):
\begin{align}\label{eq:1-switch-count}
 b(\alpha(K, D, a_{j}D+j h\sqrt{D}, j)) &= 1\land \frac{a_{j}}{h^{2}},
 \end{align}
 except that in case \( j = 1 \) and \( a_{1}D+h\sqrt D= 1 \) we set it to
 \(  a_{1}D \) when the latter is smaller.
Let \(  b(\alpha(K,D,k,j))=1 \) for all other \( k \).
For each transition rate matrix \( \mathbf{R} \) and function \( K\in\mathbf{K} \),
the trajectories of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}}(\mathbf{R},{B} ) \) are also trajectories of the medium obtained
by adding all these conditions defined by \( \alpha(K,D,\dots) \), \( b(\alpha(\dots)) \).
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The number of \( K \)-switching times during \( (u,u+D] \) is dominated by a
  Poisson random variable \( X_{1} \) with parameter \( a_{1}D \).
  We use approximation as in Definition~\ref{def:discr-approx}.
  Thus, for a sufficiently small \( \delta>0 \), let \( M_{\delta}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{PCA\/}}}(\mathbf{P},{B} ,\delta) \) with
  \( \mathbf{P}(s,{\mathbf{r}})=\mathbf{R}(s,{\mathbf{r}}) \delta \) when \( s\ne r_{0} \) and
  \( 1-\delta\sum_{s'\ne r_{0}}\mathbf{R}(s',{\mathbf{r}}) \) otherwise.
  If \( A(D,\delta) \) is the random variable counting the number of switches in \( M_{\delta} \)
  during \( (u,u+D] \) then it is clearly dominated by the random variable \( B (D,\delta) \)
  that is the number of switches when a switch takes place with probability \( a_{1}\delta\) every time.
  As \( \delta\to 0 \) the distribution of this variable \( B(D,\delta) \) converges to that of \( X_{1} \), which then
  dominates the number of \( K \)-switching times.
  Similarly, the number of \( K \)-switching times dominates
  a Poisson random variable \( X_{-1} \) with parameter \( a_{-1}D \).
    The mean and variance of \( X_{1} \) is \( a_{1}D \), hence by the Chebyshev
  inequality
  \begin{align*}
  \operatorname{\mathsf P}\mathopen\{\verythinmathskipX_{1}\ge a_{1}D + h \sqrt D\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}\le \frac{a_{1}D}{h^{2}D}= \frac{a_{1}}{h^{2}}.
  \end{align*}
  Similarly, 
\( \operatorname{\mathsf P}\mathopen\{\verythinmathskipX_{-1}\le a_{-1}D - h\sqrt D\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}\le \frac{a_{1}}{h^{2}} \).
  In the special case when \( a_{1}D+h\sqrt D = 1 \) we have the simpler bound
  \( \operatorname{\mathsf P}\mathopen\{\verythinmathskipX_{1}\ge 1\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} = 1-e^{-a_{1}D}< a_{1}D \).
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-68: body_md -->
We say that the number \( {T_{\bullet}}>0 \)\gloprocthm:cap@\( {T_{\bullet}},T^{\bullet} \).))) is a
 \emph{dwell period lower bound}\index{period!dwell!lower bound} of a
history \( \eta \) if no dwell period of \( \eta \) is shorter
than \( {T_{\bullet}} \).
<!-- end definition-68 -->
<!-- definition-69: body_md -->
The medium \gloprocprimvar@\( -var \).))) 
 \[
   -var(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}, {B} , {T_{\bullet}}, T^{\bullet}, \varepsilon).
 \]
is defined as follows.
The set \( {\mathbb{S}} \) of states is implicit in the transition function therefore
from now on, it will be omitted.
We have dwell period lower and upper bounds \( {T_{\bullet}}\leT^{\bullet} \) and
a failure probability bound \( \varepsilon>0 \).
The local state, as in Example~\ref{xmp:rand-gen}, is a record with two
fields, \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}} \) where \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}} \) consists of a single bit.
To simplify the upper-bounding of dwell periods, we assume that the
transition function has the property
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:prim-time-mark}
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1}).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}}\ne r_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}},
\end{equation}
that is the deterministic part of a cell will change at every transition.
In a more general setting later this will be called ``time marking'', see
Condition~\ref{cond:time-mark}.
For a history \( \eta \), site \( x \) let \( a \ge 0 \) be a rational number.
If \( a>0 \) then
let \( \sigma_{1}=\sigma_{1}(x,a,\eta) \), and \( \sigma_{2} \) be the first and second
switching times \( t>a \) of \( \eta \) in \( x \).
If \( a=0 \) then let \( \sigma_{1}=0 \) and let \( \sigma_{2} \) be the first switching time
\( >0 \).
Let us list the different types of local condition.
 \begin{cjenum}

  \item\label{i:prim-var.dwell-lb}
  Conditions of type \( \alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{dw-p-lb\/}}}) \) imposing \( {T_{\bullet}} \) as a
dwell period lower bound.
  We have \(  b(\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{dw-p-lb\/}}}))=\varepsilon \), and 
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{dw-p-lb\/}}}),\; \{x\}\times(a,a+T^{\bullet}],\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \]
  is the event that \( \eta(x,t) \) has two switching times
closer than \( {T_{\bullet}} \) to each other during \( (a,a+{T_{\bullet}}] \).

  \item\label{i:prim-var.dwell-ub}
  Conditions of type \( \alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{dw-p-ub\/}}}) \) imposing \( T^{\bullet} \) as a
dwell period upper bound.
  We have \(  b(\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{dw-p-ub\/}}}))=\varepsilon \), and 
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{dw-p-ub\/}}}),\;\{x\}\times(a,a+T^{\bullet}],\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \]
  is the event that \( \eta(x,t) \) has no switching times
in \( (a,a+T^{\bullet}] \).

  \item\label{i:prim-var.trans}
  Conditions of type \( \alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{comput\/}}}) \) saying that the new value of the
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}} \) field at a switching time obeys the transition function.
  We have \(  b(\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{comput\/}}})) = \varepsilon \), and
 \begin{multline*}
 {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{comput\/}}}),\; \{x\}\times(a,a+2T^{\bullet}],\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \\ = \{\eta(x,\sigma_{2}).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}}\not\in
  \mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\overline{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}}(\eta,x,t,{B} ).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}} : t\in(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}-{T_{\bullet}}/2]\mskip 1mu\mathclose\}\}.
 \end{multline*}
  Here we used the notation~\eqref{eq:trans-B}.

 \item\label{i:prim-var.coin}
  Conditions of type \( \alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{coin\/}}},j) \) for \( j=0,1 \) saying that the new
value of the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}} \) field at a switching time is obtained nearly by a
fresh coin-toss:
 \begin{alignat*}{3}
     & b(\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{coin\/}}},j)) &&= 0.5 + \varepsilon,
\\ &{g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{coin\/}}},j),\; \{x\}\times[a,a+2T^{\bullet}],\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)} &&=
 \{\eta(x,\sigma_{2}).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}} = j\}.
 \end{alignat*}
 When there is no \( \sigma_{2} \) then \( {g}(\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{coin\/}}},j),\cdot,\cdot)=0 \), so
this condition has no effect.

 \end{cjenum}
<!-- end definition-69 -->
<!-- example-19: body_md -->
All trajectories of the ordinary deterministic cellular automaton
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}},{B} ,{T} ) \) are also strong trajectories of
\( -var(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}},{B} ,{T} ,{T} ,0) \).
<!-- end example-19 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\index{theorem@Theorem!\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}} \)-simulation}
 \label{thm:sim-by-cont-pca}
  For medium
 \[
  M=-var(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}},1,{T_{\bullet}},1,\varepsilon)
 \]
  with~\eqref{eq:prim-time-mark} and \( {T_{\bullet}}<1 \) there is a noisy
transition rate \( \mathbf{R}(s,{\mathbf{r}}) \) over some state space \( {\mathbb{S}}' \) and a function
\( \pi:{\mathbb{S}}'\to{\mathbb{S}} \) such that \( \pi(\eta(x,t)) \) is a strong trajectory of \( M \) for each
trajectory \( \eta \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}}(\mathbf{R},1) \).
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The proof for trajectories is a straightforward application of
  Proposition~\ref{propo:time-bounds}, and could be modified with some
  formalism to hold also for strong trajectories.
For an appropriate \( n \) to be chosen later, let
\( {\mathbb{S}}'={\mathbb{S}}^3\times\{0,\dots,3n-1\} \).
  If \( s'=({\mathbf{s}},i) \) where \( {\mathbf{s}}=(s_{-1},s_{0},s_{1}) \) then let
\( \pi(s')=s_{0} \).
  Let us define the transition rates \( \mathbf{R}_{n}(\cdot,\cdot) \) with
\( \sum_{s'}\mathbf{R}_{n}(s',{\mathbf{r}})=3n \).
  Let \( \mathbf{K}=\mathbf{K}_{n} \) be the set of functions as defined in~\eqref{eq:K-def}
belonging to this set of states, assuming that all transition rates are positive.
Choose the function \( K\in\mathbf{K} \) as follows.
For \( {\mathbf{r}}\in({\mathbb{S}}')^{3} \) where \( r_{0}=({\mathbf{q}},i) \), where \( {\mathbf{q}}=(q_{-1},q_{0},q_{1}) \),
let \( K({\mathbf{r}}) \), be the set of those \( (\bar{\mathbf{q}},i+1) \) for which \( \bar{\mathbf{q}} \) is
given as follows.
  If \( i\ne n-1,3n-1 \) then \( \bar{\mathbf{q}}= {\mathbf{q}} \).
  If \( i=n-1 \) then \( \bar q_{j}=\pi(r_{j}) \), \( j=-1,0,1 \).
  Suppose \( i=3n-1 \): then \( \bar q_{j}= q_{j} \) for \( j=-1,1 \) and
 \( \bar q_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}({\mathbf{q}}) \).
  This completes the definition of \( K \) which is a one-element set whenever
\( i\ne 3n-1 \); in the latter case it is a two-element set, with the two elements
differing by the value of \( \bar q_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}} \).

  Now \( \mathbf{R}_{n} \) is given as follows.
\( \mathbf{R}_{n}(s,{\mathbf{r}})=0 \) for all \( s\ne K({\mathbf{r}}) \) and
\( \mathbf{R}(K({\mathbf{r}}),{\mathbf{r}})=3n \).
  This determines \( \mathbf{R}_{n}(s,{\mathbf{r}}) \) for all cases when \( K({\mathbf{r}}) \) is a
one-element set.
  If \( K({\mathbf{r}}) \) is a two-element set then the transition rates into each of
these elements are equal.
  This completes the definition of \( \mathbf{R}_{n} \).
  Thus, in a trajectory \( \eta \) of \( \mathbf{R}_{n} \), each dwell period of
  \( \pi(\eta) \) consists of \( 3n \) small dwell periods of \( \eta \).
  There is a change only in  the \( n \)th and \( 3n \)th transition.
  In the \( n \)-th transition, cell \( x \) learns the current represented
state \( \pi(\eta(x+j,t)) \) of its two neighbors.
  In the \( 3n \)-th transition, it switches its own represented state
according to the transition probabilities corresponding to the triple
of \( {\mathbb{S}} \) states it currently knows about.
  The actual transition rates \( \mathbf{R} \) differ from \( \mathbf{R}_{n} \) in an arbitrary
way by some small amount \( <\varepsilon' \).
  Let us show that we can choose first \( n \) and then \( \varepsilon' \) in such a way
that the process \( \pi(\eta) \) becomes a trajectory of \( M \).

  Let \( K_{0}({\mathbf{r}})={\mathbb{S}}\setminus(K({\mathbf{r}})\cup\{r_{0}\}) \).
  A trajectory \( \eta \) of \( \mathbf{R}_{n} \), in any switching point \( (x,t) \) makes a
switch into the set \( K(x,t-,\eta) \).
If a trajectory \( \eta \) of \( \mathbf{R} \) in a switching point \( (x,t) \)
does not switch into \( K(x,t-,\eta) \) we will this a \emph{faulty switch}.
Then it switches into
\( K_{0}(x,t-,\eta) \), but with a rate smaller than \( \varepsilon'|{\mathbb{S}}| \).
  According to the part of Proposition~\ref{propo:time-bounds}
referring to bounds of the kind~\eqref{eq:1-switch-count}, by making
\( \varepsilon' \) small enough we can always achieve that the following condition
type \( \alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{fault\/}}}) \) can be added to the others:
 \[
   b(\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{fault\/}}})) = c\varepsilon,
 \]
  where \( c \) is any positive constant chosen in advance and
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{fault\/}}}),\;\{x\}\times(a,a+2],\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \]
  is the event that a faulty switch occurs in \( x \) during \( (a,a+2] \).
  Therefore in all the local conditions for the simulated \( -var() \),
when bounding the probabilities in local conditions, we can confine
ourselves to the case that no faulty switch occurs in \( x \) during 
\( (a,a+2] \).

  Consider the conditions in~\ref{i:prim-var.dwell-lb}.
  Since we can exclude faulty switches in the time period \( (a,a+1] \), a
trajectory \( \eta(x,t) \) of \( \mathbf{R} \) will be such that when denoting
 \( \eta(x,t)=({\mathbf{r}}(x,t),i(x,t)) \), then \( i(x,t) \) increases by 1 modulo \( 3n \) in
every switch.
  Therefore there are exactly \( 3n \) switching times of \( \eta \) between any
two switching times of \( \pi(\eta) \).
  Let \( d=(1-{T_{\bullet}})/2 \).
  If \( \pi(\eta) \) has two switching times \( \sigma_{1}<\sigma_{2} \) during
\( (a,a+1] \) that are closer then \( {T_{\bullet}} \) then either they are in \( (a,a+1-d] \) or
in \( (a+d,a+1] \).
  Consider the first case, the second case is similar.
  Then \( \eta \) has at least \( 3n \) switching times during \( (a,a+1-d] \).
  By choosing \( n \) large enough and noting that the rate of \( \mathbf{R} \) is
(arbitrarily close to) \( 3n \), we can use Proposition~\ref{propo:time-bounds} to
bound the probability of this event by \( \varepsilon/3 \).
  The probability for the other case can also bounded by \( \varepsilon/3 \) and the
probability of a faulty switch can also bounded by \( \varepsilon/3 \).
  We thus get the bound \( \varepsilon \) in the conditions~\ref{i:prim-var.dwell-lb}
by canonical simulation.
A similar reasoning handles condition~\ref{i:prim-var.dwell-ub}.

  Now consider condition~\ref{i:prim-var.trans}.
  Again, we can assume that no faulty switch occurs during \( (a,a+2] \).
  There are exactly \( 3n \) switching times of \( \eta \) between \( \sigma_{1} \) and
\( \sigma_{2} \).
  According to the definition of \( \mathbf{R}_{n} \), the transition will occur
according to \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \), with the neighbor values that were read at the \( n \)th
switching time.
  Now an argument similar to the proof of~\ref{i:prim-var.dwell-lb} shows
that this \( n \)th switching time is in \( (\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}-{T_{\bullet}}/2] \).

  Finally, the possibility of adding condition~\ref{i:prim-var.coin} on
\( \pi(\eta) \) is a straightforward consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:cont-stop}.
  Indeed, let \( K'({\mathbf{r}})={\mathbb{S}}\setminus \{r_{0}\} \) and let \( K''({\mathbf{r}}) \) be the set of
elements \( ({\mathbf{q}},0)\in K'({\mathbf{r}}) \).
  Thus, jumping into \( K'' \) means making a switch in \( \pi(\eta) \).
  At that switch, the transition rates into the possibility \( q_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}}=1 \)
and \( q_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}}=0 \) are within \( \varepsilon' \) of \( 1/2 \).
  Therefore Theorem~\ref{thm:cont-stop} is applicable.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:1dim.nonerg.var}
    Theorem~\ref{thm:1dim.nonerg} also holds 
    when we allow a perturbed primitive variable-period medium
    \( -var(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}',1, 0.5, 1,\varepsilon) \) with strong trajectories
    instead of a  perturbed discrete-time cellular automaton.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:1dim.stor.var}
   Theorem~\ref{thm:remember-inf}
also holds (with the same encoding \( \psi_{*} \)) and strong trajectories
when we allow a primitive variable-period perturbation instead of a discrete-time perturbation.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:1dim.comp.var}
    Theorem~\ref{thm:1dim.comp.finite} holds (with the same encoding \( \psi_{*} \))
    also with \( -var(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}',1, 0.5, 1,\varepsilon) \) and strong trajectories
    in place of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}_{\varepsilon}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}') \).
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{crl:ipc}
  In Theorems~\ref{thm:1dim.nonerg.var}, \ref{thm:1dim.stor.var},
\ref{thm:1dim.comp.var}, we can replace \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}' \) with a rate matrix \( \mathbf{R} \),
and \( -var(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}',1,{T_{\bullet}},1,\varepsilon) \) with a \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CCA\/}}} \) with rates coming from
an arbitrary \( \varepsilon \)-perturbation of \( \mathbf{R} \).
  This proves, in particular, Theorem~\ref{thm:1dim.nonerg.cont}.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- definition-70: body_md -->
We define the \emph{totally asynchronous cellular
automaton}\index{cellular automaton!totally asynchronous} 
 \gloprocaca@$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{ACA\/}}}$.)))  
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{ACA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}})=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{ACA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}},1,1)
 \]
  associated with transition function $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}$ as follows: $\eta$ is a
trajectory if for all $x,t$ we have either $\eta(x,t+1)=\eta(x,t)$ or the
usual
 \[
   \eta(x,t+1)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\eta(x-1,t),\eta(x,t),\eta(x+1,t)).
 \]
<!-- end definition-70 -->
<!-- definition-71: body_md -->
A site $x$ is \emph{free}\index{site!free} in a configuration $\xi$ if
$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\xi(x-1),\xi(x),\xi(x+1))\ne \xi(x)$.
The set of free sites will be denoted by $L(\xi)$\gloproclem:cap@$L(\xi)$.))). 
For a space configuration $\xi$ and a set $E$ of sites, let us define the
new configuration $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\xi,E)$\gloproctr@$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\xi,E)$.))) by
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\xi,E)(x) = \begin{cases}
    \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\xi(x-1),\xi(x),\xi(x+1))    &\text{if $x\in E$}
\\  \xi(x)                              &\text{otherwise.}
  \end{cases}
 \]
<!-- end definition-71 -->
<!-- definition-72: body_md -->
Let the \emph{update set}\index{update!set} 
 \gloprocu.cap@$U(t,\eta)$.))) 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:asynch-sim.ute}
  U(t,\eta)
 \end{equation}
 be the set of sites $x$ with $\eta(x,t+1)\ne \eta(x,t)$.
<!-- end definition-72 -->
<!-- notation-4: body_md -->
For any set $A$, let us use the indicator function 
 \gloproch.greek@$\chi(x,A)$.))) 
 \[
   \chi(x,A)=\begin{cases}
   1 &\text{if $x\in A$,}
\\ 0 &\text{otherwise.}
             \end{cases}
 \]
<!-- end notation-4 -->
<!-- definition-73: body_md -->
For given history \( \eta \), we define the function
\( \tau(x,t)=\tau(x,t,\eta) \)\gloprocthm:greek@\( \tau(x,t) \).))) as follows:
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:tau-x-t}
 \begin{alignedat}{3}
       &\tau(x,0)   &&= 0,
\\    &\tau(x,t+1) &&= \tau(x,t)+ \chi(x,U(t,\eta)).
 \end{alignedat}
 \end{equation}
  We can call \( \tau(x,t) \) the \emph{effective age}\index{age!effective} of
\( x \) in \( \eta \) at time \( t \): this is the number of effective updatings that
\( x \) underwent until time \( t \).
<!-- end definition-73 -->
<!-- definition-74: body_md -->
\label{def:invar-hist}
Given a transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) and an initial configuration \( \xi \),
we say that the function \emph{has invariant histories}\index{invariant
histories} if there is a function \( \zeta(x,u)=\zeta(x,u,\xi) \) such that for all
trajectories \( \eta(x,t) \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{ACA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}) \) with \( \eta(\cdot,0)=\xi \) we have
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:t.commut}
   \eta(x,t) = \zeta(x,\tau(x,t,\eta),\xi).
 \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-74 -->
<!-- notation-5: body_md -->
Denote
 \[
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\xi,E,F)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\xi,E),F).
 \]
<!-- end notation-5 -->
<!-- definition-75: body_md -->
\label{def:commutative}
  We call a transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \)
\emph{commutative}\index{transition function!commutative} if for all
configurations \( \xi \) and all distinct pairs \( x,y\in L(\xi) \) we have
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\xi,\{x\},\{y\}) = \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\xi,\{y\},\{x\}) \).
<!-- end definition-75 -->
<!-- notation-6: body_md -->
We will denote the smallest absolute-value remainders 
 \gloprocamod@\( \mskip-\medmuskip\mkern5mu\mathbin
  {\operator@font amod}\penalty900
  \mkern5mu\mskip-\medmuskip \).))) 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:amod}
  b \mskip-\medmuskip\mkern5mu\mathbin
  {\operator@font amod}\penalty900
  \mkern5mu\mskip-\medmuskip m
 \end{equation}
 with respect to a positive integer \( m>2 \), defined by the requirement
\( -m/2< b \mskip-\medmuskip\mkern5mu\mathbin
  {\operator@font amod}\penalty900
  \mkern5mu\mskip-\medmuskip m \le m/2 \).
<!-- end notation-6 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:asynch-sim}
 \index{theorem@Theorem!Asynchronous Simulation}
 Let \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2} \) be an arbitrary transition function with state space
\( {\mathbb{S}}_{2} \).
Then there is a commutative transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1} \) with state
space \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1}={\mathbb{S}}_{2}\times R \) (for an appropriate finite set \( R \)) with
the following property.
Each state \( s\in {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \) can be represented as \( (s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}},s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}}) \) where
\( s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}\in {\mathbb{S}}_{2} \), \( s.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}}\in R \).
Let \( \xi_{2} \) be an arbitrary configuration of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{2} \) and let \( \xi_{1} \)
be a configuration of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \) such that for all \( x \) we have
\( \xi_{1}(x).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}=\xi_{2}(x) \), \( \xi_{1}(x).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}}=0\cdots 0\in R \).
Then for the trajectory \( \eta_{1} \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1}) \), with initial
configuration \( \xi_{1} \), the function \( \eta_{1}(x,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) is a trajectory of
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2}) \).
Moreover, in \( \eta_{1} \), the state of each cell changes in each step.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let \( {U} >2 \) be a positive integer and 
 \gloproccur@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \).))) 
 \gloprocprev@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}} \).))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}
 \]
  be three fields of the states of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \), where \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \),
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}}=(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}) \).
The field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \) represents numbers mod \( {U}  \).
It will be used to keep track of the time of the simulated cells mod
\( {U}  \), while \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}} \) holds the value of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \) for the previous value of
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \).

Define \( s' = \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1}(s_{-1},s_{0},s_{1}) \).
If there is a \( j\in\{-1,1\} \) with
\( (s_{j}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}-s_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}) \mskip-\medmuskip\mkern5mu\mathbin
  {\operator@font amod}\penalty900
  \mkern5mu\mskip-\medmuskip {U}  < 0 \) (that is some neighbor lags behind)
then \( s'=s_{0} \) that is there is no effect.
Otherwise, let \( r_{0}=s_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \), and for \( j=-1,1 \), let \( r_{j} \) be equal
to \( s_{j}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \) if \( s_{j}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}=s_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \), and \( s_{j}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}} \) otherwise.
 \begin{alignat*}{3}
       &s'.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}}  &&= \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2}(r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1}),
 \\  &s'.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}} &&= s_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}},
 \\  &s'.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}  &&= s_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} + 1 \bmod {U} .
 \end{alignat*}
  Thus, we use the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}} \) fields of the neighbors
according to their meaning and update the three fields according to
their meaning.
It is easy to check that this transition function simulates \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2} \)
in the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \) field if we start it by putting 0 into all other fields.

Let us check that \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1} \) is commutative.
If two neighbors \( x,x+1 \) are both allowed to update then neither of them
is behind the other modulo \( {U}  \), hence they both have the same \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \) field.
Suppose that \( x \) updates before \( x+1 \).
In this case, \( x \) will use the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \) field of \( x+1 \) for
updating and put its own \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \) field into \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}} \).
Next, since now \( x \) is ``ahead'' according to \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \), cell \( x+1 \)
will use the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}} \) field of \( x \) for updating: this was the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \)
field of \( x \) before.
Therefore the effect of consecutive updating is the same as that of
simultaneous updating.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-76: body_md -->
The commutative medium of the above proof will be called the
 \emph{marching soldiers}\index{marching soldiers} scheme.
<!-- end definition-76 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{crl:var-sim}
  For every deterministic transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2} \) over some
state-space \( {\mathbb{S}}_{2} \), there is a set of states \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \), a transition
function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1} \)
over \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \), and a code that for any values \( {T_{\bullet}}_{1}\leT^{\bullet}_{1} \),
is a simulation of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2}) \) by
\( -var(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1},1,{T_{\bullet}}_{1},T^{\bullet}_{1},0) \).
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1} \) be the commutative transition function given by
Theorem~\ref{thm:asynch-sim}, with the fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}} \).
Let \( \xi_{2} \) be an arbitrary configuration of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{2} \) and let \( \xi_{1} \)
be a configuration of \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \) defined in the statement of the same
theorem. 
Let \( \eta_{1} \) be a trajectory of
\( -var(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1},1,{T_{\bullet}}_{1},T^{\bullet}_{1},0) \), with the starting configuration
\( \xi_{1} \).

An update set \( U(t,\eta_{1}) \) similar to~\eqref{eq:asynch-sim.ute} can be
defined now for the trajectory \( \eta_{1} \) as follows: \( x \) is in
\( U(t,\eta_{1}) \) iff \( t \) is a switching time of \( \eta_{1} \).
  Similarly, \( \tau(x,t,\eta_{1}) \) can be defined as in~\eqref{eq:tau-x-t}: 
 \begin{alignat*}{3}
        &\tau(x,0)   &&= 0,
\\    &\tau(x,t)   &&= \tau(x,t-)+ \chi(x,U(t,\eta_{1})).
 \end{alignat*}
 With these, let us define
 \begin{alignat*}{3}
      &\sigma(x,s,\xi)         &&= \bigwedge\mathopen\{\verythinmathskipt:\tau(x,t,\eta')=s\mskip 1mu\mathclose\},
\\  &\eta_{2}(x,s,\xi) &&= \eta_{1}(x,\sigma(x,s)).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}
 \end{alignat*}
  By the cited theorem, \( \eta_{2} \) is a trajectory of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2}) \).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- definition-77: body_md -->
For a standard computing medium with transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \), integers \( s \)
and \( t \) 
and string \( X \) consider a trajectory \( \eta \) of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}) \) over the rectangle
\( [0,s]\times[0,t] \) with an initial configuration in which
\( \eta(0,0)=\eta(s,0)=\#\cdots \# \), further \( X \) is on the input track on the interval
\( [1,s-1] \) (padded with \( * \)'s to fill up \( [1,s-1] \)), \( * \)'s on the output
track and 0's on the other tracks.
This defines a trajectory \( \eta \) since the \( \# \)'s on the input field
in cells 0 and \( s \) imply that the cells outside the interval \( [0,s] \)
will have no effect.
Assume that, at time \( t \), the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \) track has no \( * \) on the interval
\( [1,s-1] \).
The string \( w \) on the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \) track on \( [1,s-1] \) will be called the
\emph{result}\index{computation!result} of the computation, denoted by 
 \gloproctr@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(X; s, t) \).))) 
 \[
  w= \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(X; s, t).
 \]
<!-- end definition-77 -->
<!-- definition-78: body_md -->
\label{def:effic-univ}
The standard computing transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{0} \) is
 \emph{efficiently universal\/}\index{transition function!universal!efficiently}
if for every standard computing transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \), there is a
string \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{prog\/}}}} \) and constants \( c,d \) such that for all strings \( X \) and
positive integers \( s,t \) we have 
 \gloprocprog@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{prog\/}}}} \).)))  
 \[
     \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(X; s, t) = \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{0}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{prog\/}}}}\sqcup X; c\cdot s, d\cdot t)
 \]
  whenever the left-hand side is defined.
<!-- end definition-78 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
There are efficiently universal standard computing transition functions.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
This theorem can be proven similarly to Theorem~\ref{thm:univ}.
The main addition to the construction is that before \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{0} \) starts
a block simulation of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) the input will be distributed bit-by-bit to
the colonies simulating the cells of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \).
At the end, the output will be collected from these colonies.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- definition-79: body_md -->
We fix an efficiently universal standard computing transition function 
 \gloprocuniv@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}} \).))) 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:univ}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}}
 \end{equation}
  for the definition of various string functions.
In view of Theorem~\ref{thm:asynch-sim}, we can (and will) also assume that
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}} \) is commutative as in Definition~\ref{def:commutative}.
For a string function \( f(X) \) defined over some domain \( E \) we will say
that \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{prog\/}}}} \) is a program for \( f \) with
\emph{time complexity bound} \( t \) and \emph{space complexity bound \( s \) over \( E \)} if
the relation
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{prog\/}}}}\sqcup X;s,t) = f(X)
 \]
holds.
<!-- end definition-79 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:self-simul}
Let us denote the output  of a universal machine (it does not matter, whether it
is a Turing machine or cellular automaton) computing the universal  partial
recursive function \( u(p,x) \), where
\( p \) is the program, and \( x \) is the input.
Let \( \tau \) be an arbitrary computable transformation of strings into strings.
Kleene's Fixpoint Theorem (Recursion Theorem) says that there is a program \( q \)
with the property that for all \( x \) we have \( u(q,x)=u(\tau(p),x) \).
What does this theorem have to do with our problem of self-simulation?
Suppose that we have some program \( p \), and a transformation \( \tau(p) \) of \( p \)
that carries out a simulation of the action of \( p \), with possibly some
modifications and extra properties (say, error-corrections, and the change of
some parameters).
The theorem says that there is a program \( q \) which already acts as \( \tau(q) \).

One  intuitive proof of the fixpoint theorem goes as follows.
Assume that we have a programming language that has at least the  following
ingredients: 1) We can define functions (procedures) in it.
2) It contains a function \( \mathtt{U(p,x)} \) that computes \( u(p,x) \), that is it interprets
the string \( p \) as a program on input \( x \).
3) It contains a function \( \mathtt{MyText()} \),\footnote{The parentheses
\( \mathtt{()} \), used for example in the programming language C, 
are a useful reminder that even when it has no explicit arguments, the function
depends on the internal state of the machine at the time of execution.} 
which returns the string that is the text of the program.
One implementation of such a function in a modern computer uses the fact that
the program is stored at some standard place in memory: it is enough to go there
and read it out.
Let \( \mathtt{T(p)} \) be the expression of the transformation \( \tau(p) \) in our
programming language: then the fixedpoint program is
 \begin{align*}
  q=\mathtt{U(T(MyText()),x)}
 \end{align*}
(the \( \mathtt{x} \) in the program is just a symbol in the program, not something
the program \( q \) depends on).
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- notation-7: body_md -->
\label{n:neighbors}
For a field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \), if \( \eta \) is the current configuration and \( x \) is a site
then we will sometimes write
 \begin{align*}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}(x) \text{ for } \eta.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}(x).
 \end{align*}
  We will write 
 \gloprocth.greek@\( \vartheta_{j}(x) \).))) 
 \[
 \vartheta_{j}(x) = x + j{B} 
 \]
 for the site \( j \) steps from site \( x \).
In a semi-formal description of a rule, \( {\mathbf{x}} \)\gloprocx@\( {\mathbf{x}} \).))) refers to the
cell to which it is applied (the ``current'' cell).
In the condition as well as the action of the rule, a field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}({\mathbf{x}})=\eta.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}({\mathbf{x}}) \)
will simply be written as \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \).
Denote 
 \gloprocf.cap@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}^{j} \).))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}^{j}=\eta.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}(\vartheta_{j}({\mathbf{x}})).
 \]
<!-- end notation-7 -->
<!-- definition-80: body_md -->
\label{def:rule}
An \emph{elementary rule} has the following form:

\begin{algo}[H]
 \If{\( C_{1} \) \text{\textnormal{\textsf{\bfseries and}}\unskip } \( \dotsm \) \text{\textnormal{\textsf{\bfseries and}}\unskip } \( C_{k} \)}{
       \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \gets f(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1}^{j_{1}},\dots,\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{n}^{j_{n}} \))
  }  
\end{algo}

\begin{sloppypar}
  Here \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{i} \) are fields (possibly specified as bit segments like in~\eqref{eq:F[i:j]}),
 \( j_{i}\in\mathopen\{-1,0,1\mathclose\} \).
Each of the conditions \( C_{i} \) has the form
