\( a_{1}\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1}^{j_{1}}+\dots+a_{n}\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{n}^{j_{n}}\le b \)
with integer constants \( a_{i}, b \).
(When the condition is not applicable, the rule does not change the state.)
The function \( f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\) must be computable on \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}} \)
in linear time.
This allows for many functions: for example, if \( x ,y \) are integers in binary notation then
\( x\cdot y \), \( {\lfloor x/y\rfloor} \), \( x\bmod y \) are all computable in linear time by known
cellular automata algorithms, see for example~\cite{Leighton92}.
\end{sloppypar}

A \emph{rule} is a sequence of elementary rules.
The transition function will be defined by a set of rules.
In case some rules contradict each other, they will be ordered by explicit \emph{priority}.
Rules will sometimes be associated with certain fields.
The lowest-priority rule referring to a field is called the
\emph{default}\index{rule!default}.
<!-- end definition-80 -->
<!-- definition-81: body_md -->
\label{def:combination}
When a sequence of rules is combined, this is a \emph{parallel}
combination: all the rules apply to the same transition,
and do not refer to consecutive times.
Sometimes we may use the notation
 \gloproc"+@\( \texttt{;},\hbox{$\mskip\medmuskip\parallel\mskip\medmuskip$} \).))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{R\/}}}}_{1}\hbox{$\mskip\medmuskip\parallel\mskip\medmuskip$} \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{R\/}}}}_{2} \hbox{$\mskip\medmuskip\parallel\mskip\medmuskip$} \dots \hbox{$\mskip\medmuskip\parallel\mskip\medmuskip$} \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{R\/}}}}_{n}
 \]
  for a combination of \( n \) rules.
As a shorthand, we may also combine rules in series:
the rule
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{R\/}}}}_{1};\ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{R\/}}}}_{2}
 \]
  asks for carrying out the rules \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{R\/}}}}_{1} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{R\/}}}}_{2} \)
consecutively.
This can be understood in terms of a field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \) which
we are always going to have and can be replaced with a conditional.

In both parallel and serial combination,  we will refer to 
the rules \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{R\/}}}}_{i} \) as \emph{sub-rules}, when they
will always be invoked (``called'') by other rules.
Still, for a better flow of discussion we will frequently refer to sub-rules
as just ``rules''.
Sub-rules may have \emph{parameters} that are specified at the time of the call.
Rule \( P(i) \) with parameter \( i \) can be viewed as a different rule for
each possible value of \( i \).
<!-- end definition-81 -->
<!-- definition-82: body_md -->
Sometimes the conditions of a conditional statement
are indexed in a regular way, then we may use the shorthand 
\( \textbf{cfor} \)\gloproccfor@\( \textbf{cfor} \).))) as below:

\begin{algo}
    \cFor{\( j\in\{-1,1\} \)}{
      \If{\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}^{j}=0 \)}{
               \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}\gets 0 \)
    }
  }
\end{algo}
So this rule tests the conditions in order,
carries out the command of the first satisfied condition and skips the rest.
Several conditions that are to be tested one after the other
will be combined using the construct \textbf{cond}.
This can be seen as an alternative to the
``\textbf{if}\( \dots \)\textbf{then}\( \dots \)\textbf{elsif}\( \dots \)''
construct.

\begin{algo}[H]
\Cond{
    \cFor{\( j\in\{-1,1\} \)}{
      \If{\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}^{j}=0 \)}{
               \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}\gets 0 \)
       }
    }
    \cFor{\( j\in\{-1,1\} \)}{
      \If{\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}^{j}\not\equiv\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}+j\pmod{{U} } \)}{
               \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}\gets\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Latent\/}}} \)
       }
     }
 }
\end{algo}

Both the parallel and the consecutive combination of rules can be over an
indexed set, and then we get the constructs \textbf{pfor} and \textbf{for}:

 \begin{algo}[H]
   \pFor{\( (k,d)\in\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Mail-ind\/}}} \)}{
      \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}_{k,d}\gets \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Mail-to-receive\/}}}(k,d) \)
     }
   \end{algo}
   
Here, \gloprocpfor@\( \texttt{pfor} \).))) 
the rule is carried out simultaneously for all fields
indexed by the indicated values \( k \).
\gloprocfor@\textbf{for}.))) 
On the other hand in the \( \textbf{for} \) example  the application is consecutive:

  \begin{algo}[H]
   \For{\( i=a \) \KwTo \( b \)}{
      \( {\mathopen\langle \text{some rule referring to } i\mathclose\rangle} \)
   }
  \end{algo}

Another use of \( \textbf{for} \) can be this:

\begin{algo}[H]
   \For{\( n \) steps of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \)}{
      \( {\mathopen\langle \cdots\mathclose\rangle} \)
   }
 \end{algo}
 which, started at some \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}=t \) will mean that the commands \( {\mathopen\langle \cdots\mathclose\rangle} \) will
 run under the condition \( t_{1}\le\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}<t+n \).
  \gloprocrepeat@\textbf{repeat}.))) 
The \textbf{repeat} construct could be translated into a \textbf{for}:

  \begin{algo}[H]
  \pRepeat{\( k \)}{
     \( {\mathopen\langle \cdots\mathclose\rangle} \)
   }
 \end{algo}
<!-- end definition-82 -->
<!-- definition-83: body_md -->
We may use temporary constants or functions in the course of defining a
rule, as in this example:

  \gloproclet@\texttt{let}.))) 
 \begin{algo}
  \text{\textnormal{\textsf{\bfseries let}}\unskip } \( f(i)\gets\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}+\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}^{i} \)
\end{algo}
<!-- end definition-83 -->
<!-- example-20: body_md -->
\gloprocmarch@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{March\/}}}}_{0} \).))) 
  Here is a description of the transition function given in the proof
of Theorem~\ref{thm:asynch-sim} (Asynchronous Simulation). 

 \begin{algo}\caption{rule \( \protect\ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{March\/}}}}_{0} \)}\label{alg:March0}
   \pFor{\( j\in\{-1,0,1\} \)}{
      \text{\textnormal{\textsf{\bfseries let}}\unskip } \( r(j)\gets\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}}^{j} \) if  \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}^{j}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \), and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}}^{j} \) otherwise
    }
    \If{\( \cmforall\, j\in\{-1,1\}\;(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}^{j}-\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}) \mskip-\medmuskip\mkern5mu\mathbin
  {\operator@font amod}\penalty900
  \mkern5mu\mskip-\medmuskip {U}  \ge 0 \)}{
       \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Prev\/}}}} \gets  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \)\;
       \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cur\/}}}} \gets  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2}(r(-1),r(0),r(1)) \)\;
       \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \gets  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} + 1 \bmod {U}  \)
       }
 \end{algo}
<!-- end example-20 -->
<!-- definition-84: body_md -->
A \emph{location}\index{location} is defined by a pair \( (\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}},I) \) where \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) is a field,
and \( I \) is an interval of addresses in the colony, or by a constant-size union of such pairs
\( (\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{j},I_{j}) \).
  We will denote the  track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) over interval \( I \) as 
 \gloprocf.cap@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}(I) \).))) 
 \[
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}(I).
 \]
The name of a location will generally begin with an underscore, like
 \[
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Info\/}}}}.
 \]
The set of addresses (typically an interval) of a location \( L \) will be denoted by \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{space\/}}}(L) \).
<!-- end definition-84 -->
<!-- definition-85: body_md -->
The location on the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) track containing the represented string is denoted by
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Info\/}}}} \).\gloprocinfo.loc@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Info\/}}}} \).)))
<!-- end definition-85 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
Occasionally, we may treat the union of two or three locations as one.
It is easy to generalize the rules dealing with locations to this case.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-86: body_md -->
\label{def:Param}
The rule language can contain some definitions of names for constant
strings of symbols, of the form 
 \gloprocparam@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}} \).))) 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:Param}
 \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}}_{1}=s_{1},\;\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}}_{2}=s_{2},\dots
 \end{equation}
  where \( s_{i} \) are some strings.
The names \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}}_{i} \) are allowed to be used in the rules.
This has the advantage that even if we use, say, \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}}_{1} \) twice in a rule,
this does not make the rule much longer, even if the value of the 
parameter is a long string.

Parameters will have descriptive names: say, we might write 
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Height\/}}} \) for \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}}_{1} \),
when \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}}_{1} \) indicates the level in a hierarchy of simulations.
Parameters will always be used via the function 
 \begin{align*}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Write-param\/}}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{loc\/}}}),
 \end{align*}
which writes the string value of parameter \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}} \) to location \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{loc\/}}} \).
This can be implemented as a subrule, via the primitive access function 
 \begin{align*}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Param\/}}}_{i}(j),
 \end{align*}
referring to the \( j \)th symbol of parameter \( i \).
There will also be a special parameter: 
 \begin{align*}
\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{My-rules\/}}},
 \end{align*}
whose value is the string that is the sequence of all the rules.
This will implement self-reference in the style of Remark~\ref{rem:self-simul}.
<!-- end definition-86 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:rule-lang}
 \index{theorem@Theorem!Rule Language}
  There is a string \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Interpr\/}}} \)\gloprocinterpr@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Interpr\/}}} \).))) and an
integer \( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{interpr-coe}}}} \)\gloprocinterpr@\( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{interpr-coe}}}} \).))) such that the
following holds.
If string \( P \) is a description of a transition rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}} \) over state
set \( {\mathbb{S}} \) in the above language (along with the necessary parameters), then
the machine \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}} \) defined in~\eqref{eq:univ} computes
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1}) \) (possibly padded with \( * \)'s) from
 \[
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Interpr\/}}}\sqcup P\sqcup r_{-1}\sqcup r_{0}\sqcup r_{1}
 \]
 within computation time \( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{interpr-coe}}}}(|P|+1)^{2}{\lVert {\mathbb{S}}\rVert} \) and space
\( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{interpr-coe}}}}(|P|+{\lVert {\mathbb{S}}\rVert}+1) \).
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- definition-87: body_md -->
The rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Retrieve\/}}}} \) uses the locations \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Retrieved\/}}}}_{m} \) to deposit the
string it retrieves from the neighbor colony number \( m\in\{-1,0,1\} \).
<!-- end definition-87 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:variable-width-copy}
Here we assumed that the source and destination locations are on tracks of the same width,
and have the same lengths.
We can write a more general version of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Copy\/}}}} \) using a loop.
For example assume that the source location, of length \( n \),
is on a track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) that is 5 times wider than its destination location
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}} \) of length \( 5 n \).
                                                                        
          
                
                                                                  
              
Then we can split the field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) into 5 sub-fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1},\dots,\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{5} \).
More generally, a track that has \( m \) times the width can be
treated as into \( m \) tracks of the same width.
Here \( m \) can even be a variable computed from the widths of the fields in question,
using the primitive \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}[i\mathord{:} j] \) as defined in~\eqref{eq:F[i:j]}.
We can do the copying in 5 iterations, copying each sub-track separately,
or (this will be our actual choice later)
we can post each cell onto the mail track in 5 steps.
The rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Move-mail\/}}}} \) can proceed in parallel with all these iterations.

Similarly, one can write a program for copying
a longer and narrower location into a shorter and wider one.
Also, instead of giving the locations as arguments, we may just give the name of a
field where they are described.  
In applications we will assume this more general implementation.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- definition-88: body_md -->
\label{def:indirect-copy}
  The description \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{1}(\left[a_{1},a_{2}\right)) \) of a location can fit into a
single field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}}_{1} \) of some cell.
If for example argument \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{loc\/}}}_{1} \) of the rule
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Copy\/}}}}(m,\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{loc\/}}}_{1},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{loc\/}}}_{2}) \) is given by a field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}}_{1} \) 
this way, then we write \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Copy\/}}}}(m,\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}}_{1}*,\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{loc\/}}}_{2}) \).
This will only happen if \( m=0 \), that is the copying proceeds within one
colony.
It will be assumed that field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}}_{1} \) of
each cell of the colony contains the same information \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{loc\/}}}_{1} \).
Therefore the rule can be written just as above, except that
some of its parameters are read now from the field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G\/}}}}_{1} \).
<!-- end definition-88 -->
<!-- definition-89: body_md -->
\label{def:eval-locations}
Here are a few locations used in the rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Eval\/}}}} \):
\begin{bullets}
 \item Track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cpt\/}}}} \) is used for universal computation, with sub-tracks
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cpt\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cpt\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \).
 \item  The location for the interpreter on the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cpt\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Input\/}}}} \) track is
denoted by \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Interpr\/}}}} \).
  \item The location for the program to be executed by the universal medium
    \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}} \) is denoted by \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Prog\/}}}} \).
  \item The locations for the parameters of the program
    are denoted by \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Param\/}}}}_{i} \), \( i=1,2,\dots \), as needed,
  \item The location of the arguments of the function to be executed
    on the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cpt\/}}}} \) track are \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Arg\/}}}}_{m} \) for \( m\in\{-1,0,1\} \).
 \gloprocarg@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Arg\/}}}}_{m} \).)))     
  \item The location of the output of the computation on the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cpt\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Output\/}}}} \) track
    is \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Sim-output\/}}}} \)\gloprocsim-output@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Sim-output\/}}}} \).))).
We assume it to be the same interval as that of location \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Info\/}}}} \).
\end{bullets}
<!-- end definition-89 -->
<!-- definition-90: body_md -->
The encoding \( \varphi_{*} \) of a cell state \( v \) of \( M_{2} \) into a colony of
\( M_{1} \) is defined as follows.
The string \( v \) is written into \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{\_Info\/}}}} \).
The \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cpt\/}}}} \) track and the mail tracks are set to all 1's.
Each \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \) field is set to 0.  
For all \( i \), the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}} \) field of cell \( i \) of the colony is set to \( i \).
<!-- end definition-90 -->
<!-- condition-1: body_md -->
\label{cond:simple-block-sim-ineq}
The following inequalities must be obeyed.
 \begin{description}

  \item[Cell Capacity Lower Bound]\index{lower@Lower Bound!Cell Capacity}
 \[
    {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{1}\rVert} \ge c_{1}{\lceil \log {U} \rceil}+ {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}}}\rVert} + c_{2}
 \]
  where \( c_{1},c_{2} \) can be easily computed from the following
consideration. 
  What we really need is 
 \( {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{1}\rVert} \ge |\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}|+|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}|+|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}|+|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}|+|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cpt\/}}}}| \) where the following
choices can be made:
 \begin{alignat*}{3}
        &|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}|       &&= 2,
\\   &|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}_{i}|  &&= |\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}_{i}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Toaddr\/}}}}|                        
       + |\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Mail\/}}}}_{i}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}| = {\lceil \log {Q} \rceil} + 3,
\\   &|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Cpt\/}}}}|        &&= {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}}}\rVert},
\\   &|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}|      &&= |\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}| = {\lceil \log {U} \rceil}.
 \end{alignat*}

 \item[Colony Size Lower Bound]\index{lower@Lower Bound!Colony Size}
  \[
   {Q}  \ge \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{interpr-coe}}}}({\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{2}\rVert} + |\ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Trans-prog\/}}}}_{2}|
         + \log {U}  + 1).
  \]
 With the field sizes as agreed above, this provides sufficient space in
the colony for information storage and computation.

  \item[Work Period Lower Bound]\index{lower@Lower Bound!Work Period}
 \[
   {U}  \ge 3{Q} +\ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{interpr-coe}}}}(|\ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Trans-prog\/}}}}_{2}| + 1)^{2}{\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{2}\rVert}.
 \]
 With the field sizes above, this allows sufficient time for the above
program to be carried out.
 \end{description}
<!-- end condition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:simp-sim}
 \index{theorem@Theorem!Basic Block Simulation}
  There are strings \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Sim-prog\/}}}}_{1} \)\gloprocsim-prog@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Sim-prog\/}}}} \).))),
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Sim-prog\/}}}}_{0} \) such that the following holds.
If \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Trans-prog\/}}}}_{2} \) with parameters \( {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{1}\rVert} \), \( {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{2}\rVert} \), \( {Q}  \),
\( {U}  \) satisfies the above inequalities, and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Trans-prog\/}}}}_{2} \)
defines a transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2} \),
then \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Sim-prog\/}}}}_{1} \) is a rule program with parameters
 \begin{align*}
\ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Trans-prog\/}}}}_{2}, {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{1}\rVert}, {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{2}\rVert}, {Q} , {U} ,
 \end{align*}
defining a transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1} \) such that \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1}) \) 
has a block simulation of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2},{Q} ,{U} ) \).

 If \( {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{1}\rVert},{\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{2}\rVert},{Q} ,{U}  \) satisfy the above inequalities, then
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Sim-prog\/}}}}_{0} \) is a rule program with parameters
\( {\lVert {\mathbb{S}}_{1}\rVert} \), \( {Q}  \), \( {U}  \),
defining a transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1} \) such that \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1}) \) 
has a block simulation of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{CA\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1},{Q} ,{U} ) \).
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:non-adjacent}
  The paper~\cite{Gacs1dim86} used communication only between adjacent neighbors.
  It used a special mechanism for preventing accidental intrusions into an intact colony:
  growth in a zigzag pattern.
  Here this is achieved by communication between non-adjacent neighbors,
  enabling a colony of ``stronger'' cells to defend itself from
  the accidental intrusion by ``weaker'' cells.
  However, to simulate such a property on higher levels, it will also be used
  to pass information other than strength to non-adjacent neighbors.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- definition-91: body_md -->
\label{def:damage}
For the media to be defined, robust media,
we introduce a special set of states $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Bad\/}}}\subseteq\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vacant\/}}}$\gloprocbad@$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Bad\/}}}$.))).
For a history $\eta$ we define the \emph{damage set} 
 \gloprocdamage@$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}$.))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}(\eta)=\mathopen\{\mskip 1mu (x,t) : \eta(x,t)\in\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Bad\/}}}\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} .
 \]
  For a space configuration, the damage is defined similarly.
For a site $x$ a time interval $I$ is \emph{damage-free}\index{damage-free}
if $\eta(x,\cdot)$ is not in $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Bad\/}}}$ during $I$.
<!-- end definition-91 -->
<!-- definition-92: body_md -->
\label{def:damage-map}
We will use the following constants:
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:bdist}
  \gamma = 5,\quad \beta = 2\gamma+5.  
 \end{equation}
  Let us define the rectangle
 \begin{align}\label{eq:Vdam}
   V=\left[-{B} /2,{B} /2\right)\times(-T^{\bullet}/2,T^{\bullet}/2], 
 \end{align}
 then the corresponding rectangle $V^{*}$ is defined using ${B} ^{*},T^{\bullet *}$.
 Two space-time points are said to be \emph{too close} if they are contained
 in a single copy (space-time translation) of \( \betaV \).
 Two sets \( A_{1},A_{2} \) are \emph{too far} if no copy of \( \gammaV^{*} \) intersects both.
A subset $A$ of the damage is called an \emph{island} if it is covered by a translation of
$\betaV$ and is too far from the rest of damage.
In a simulation $\eta^{*}=\Phi^{*}(\eta)$ between two robust media,
the set $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}(\eta^{*})$ is obtained after we remove all islands of
$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}(\eta)$.  
We call this definition of $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}(\eta^{*})$ the \emph{damage map} of simulation
$\Phi^{*}$.
<!-- end definition-92 -->
<!-- condition-2: body_md -->
\label{cond:restor}
  Let $ b(\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{restor\/}}}))=\varepsilon$.
  Further, for any pair $(x,t)$ let
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{restor\/}}}),\; (x,t)+(\gamma+2)V,\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)}
 \]
  be the event function for the event that there is damage in
$\eta((x,t)+V)$.
<!-- end condition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:sim-damage}
 \index{lemma@Lemma!Simulation Damage Probability Bound}
  Let $M$, $M^{*}$ be media with parameters $\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon^{*}$,
with ${B} ^{*}\ge {B} $, $T^{\bullet *}\ge T^{\bullet}$, whose local
condition system includes the Restoration Property.
Let a simulation $\Phi^{*}$ be defined between them which assigns damage
in $M^{*}$ according to the damage map of Definition~\ref{def:damage-map}.
There is a constant $c_{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Dam\/}}}}$ such that if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eps*}
  \varepsilon^{*}\ge c_{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Dam\/}}}}(({B} ^{*}/{B} )(T^{\bullet *}/T^{\bullet})\varepsilon)^{2}  
\end{equation}
  then $\Phi^{*}$ is a deterministic canonical simulation map for damage, as defined 
in~\ref{sec:canonical}.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
It is enough to show an expression of the form~\eqref{eq:canonical} for
local conditions of type $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{restor\/}}}$ in $M^{*}$.
Let $\eta$ be a trajectory of $M$.
Consider the event that 
$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}(\eta^{*})$ intersects the middle part $W'=(x,t)+V^{*}$
of rectangle
\begin{align*}
 W=(x,t)+(\gamma+2)V^{*},
\end{align*}
with \( \beta,\gamma \) defined in~\eqref{eq:bdist},
then of course $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}(\eta)$ intersects it, too.
In what follows, by ``damage'' we mean the set $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}(\eta)$.
We claim that the damage in \( W \)
cannot be covered by a copy \( W'' \) of \( \betaV \).
Suppose namely that it can: then it can also be covered by a copy of \( W'+\betaV\).
However, the rectangle \( W'+\betaV \) is too far from the complement of \( W \).
Then so is \( W'' \), so it is an island and as such it would have been
deleted by the damage map, contradicting the assumption that its elements
belong to \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}^{*} \).

\begin{sloppypar}
We found two damage points $p_{1},p_{2}$ in $W$ that are not too close.
Let us fix some partition of the space into copies of \( V \).
Let \( \mathcal{V} \) be the set of those elements of this partition intersecting \( W \).
For each point $p$ in space-time, let $U(p)$ be the $U\in\mathcal{V}$ with
$p\in U$.
Let \( U'(p)=U(p)+(\gamma+1)V \).
The fact that \( p_{1},p_{2} \) are not too close implies that the two copies
\( U'(p_{1}) \) and \( U'(p_{2}) \) of \( (\gamma+2)V \) are disjoint.
Indeed, if they intersected then some copy of \( 2(\gamma+2)V \)
would contain both, but due to~\eqref{eq:bdist} then they would be too close.

Let $E$ be the set of pairs $U_{1}, U_{2}$ in $\mathcal{V}$  with \( U'_{1}\cap U'_{2}=\emptyset \).
We found
 \[
 {g}^{*}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{restor\/}}},(\gamma+2)V^{*},\eta^{*}) 
  \le \sum_{(U_{1},U_{2})\in E}\prod_{j=1,2} {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{restor\/}}},U'_{j},\eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)},
\]
therefore \( \operatorname{\mathsf{E}}  {g}^{*}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{restor\/}}},V^{*},\eta^{*}) \le |E|\varepsilon^{2} \).
Since counting bounds $|E|$ by
$c_{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Dam\/}}}} (({B} ^{*}/{B} ) (T^{\bullet *}/T^{\bullet}))^{2}$ for
an appropriate constant $c_{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Dam\/}}}}$, by the assumption~\eqref{eq:eps*}
both conditions of a weak canonical simulation in~\eqref{eq:canonical} are satisfied.
  \end{sloppypar}
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- notation-8: body_md -->
Let us fix a history $\eta$.
                                                                
                                                                        
                                                                       
                         
                                                 
                                                    
 For a (non-vacant) cell $x$, in direction \( j=\pm 1 \)
 there is at most one cell at distance smaller than $2{B} $: if it
exists and there is no damage between it and $x$ then we denote it also by \( \vartheta_{j}(x,t,\eta) \).
We will omit $\eta$, and sometimes even $t$, from the arguments when
it is obvious from the context.
By convention, whenever $\vartheta_{j}(x,t,\eta)$ is undefined then
let \( \eta(\vartheta_{j}(x,t,\eta),t)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \).
<!-- end notation-8 -->
<!-- definition-93: body_md -->
The transition function in a robust medium has the form
  \begin{align}\label{eq:rob-trans}
    \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}({\mathbf{s}},{\mathbf{a}}).
  \end{align}
 Here \( {\mathbf{s}} = (s_{-1},s_{0},s_{1}) \), \( {\mathbf{a}} =(a_{-1},a_{1}) \)
have the following meaning. 
 \( s_{0} \) is the state of the cell whose transition will happen, and for \( j=\pm 1 \)
 \( s_{j} \) is the state of its (not necessarily adjacent) neighbors in direction \( j \).
 Further \( a_{j}=1 \) if the neighbor in direction \( j \) is adjacent and 0 otherwise.
  The transition does not depend on \( a_{j} \) if either \( s_{j} \) or \( s_{0} \) is vacant.
  Note that \( a_{j} \) is in fact \( a_{j}(x,t,\eta) \), but we may omit the arguments
that are obvious from the context.
 In analogy with~\eqref{eq:trans}, let 
 \[
   \overline{\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}}(\eta,x,t)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}((\vartheta_{-1}(x),x,\vartheta_{1}(x)),(a_{-1}(x),a_{1}(x))).
 \]
The symbol $\eta$ will be omitted from $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\eta,x,t)$ when it is
obvious from the context.
<!-- end definition-93 -->
<!-- definition-94: body_md -->
\label{def:rob}
A robust medium will be denoted by 
 \gloprocrob@$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Rob\/}}}$.))) 
 \[
 \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Rob\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}, {B} ,{T_{\bullet}},T^{\bullet},\varepsilon,\varepsilon'). 
                                               
\]
The first bit of the state of a cell will be the field $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}}$;  we will write
 \begin{equation*}
 \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{All\/}}}}\setminus\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}}.
 \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-94 -->
<!-- condition-3: body_md -->
\label{cond:time-mark}
 \index{condition@Condition!Time Marking}
  If a cell is not vacant, then the transition function always changes it.
<!-- end condition-3 -->
<!-- condition-4: body_md -->
\label{cond:latent}
  Non-vacant cells will have a property (typically represented by a field) of being \emph{latent} or not.
  Newborn cells will be latent.
  The transition function will not make a difference between a vacant and latent neighbor.
<!-- end condition-4 -->
<!-- condition-5: body_md -->
\label{cond:cling}
   \index{condition@Condition!Cling to Life}
A cell will only be erased if it may disturb a close non-aligned neighbor:
namely, suppose that \( u_{0}\ne\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}({\mathbf{u}},{\mathbf{a}})=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \).
   Then there is a \( j=\pm 1 \) with \( u_{j}\ne\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \) and \( a_{j}=0 \).
<!-- end condition-5 -->
<!-- definition-95: body_md -->
\label{def:creator-emerging}
  Recall the form of the transition function in~(\ref{eq:rob-trans}).
  We will call a pair $(j,v)\in\{-1,1\}\times{\mathbb{S}}$, a
\emph{potential creator}\index{creator!potential} of a non-vacant state $s$
if $s=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}({\mathbf{u}},{\mathbf{a}})$ where \( u_{j}=v \), \( u_{0}= u_{-j}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \).
The expectation is that an adjacent cell with state \( s \) will be created by
the cell with state \( v \) determined by the state \( u_{j} \) of the creator
\emph{independently of} the state \( u_{-j} \).

Consider a history $\eta$, with a switching time $\sigma$ of cell
$x$ when $\eta(x,t)$ turns from vacant to non-vacant.
We call $y=x+j{B}$ a \emph{creator}\index{creator} of $x$ for time $\sigma$ if
$(j,\eta(y,\sigma-))$ is a potential creator of $\eta(x,\sigma)$, further
$\eta(y,t)$ is non-vacant for $t\in(\sigma-{T_{\bullet}}/2,\sigma+{T_{\bullet}})$.
(So a creator is supposed to survive the creation.)
On the other hand, if there is no
\( t \) in \( (\sigma-{T_{\bullet}}/2,\sigma] \) when the
interval\( \left[x-2{B},x+3{B}\right) \) intersects the body of any cell,
we will say that the cell \( x \) \emph{emerged} at time \( \sigma \).
<!-- end definition-95 -->
<!-- definition-96: body_md -->
\label{def:special-sw-times}
  For a history $\eta$, cell $x$ and number $a \ge 0$ let
 \[
  \sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\sigma_{0}
 \]
  be defined as follows.
  The values $\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}$ are the first two switching times of \( x \)
  in $(a,a+2T^{\bullet}]$, but \( \sigma_{2} \) is defined only if $\eta(x,\sigma_{1})$ is non-vacant.
0 is considered a switching time if $\eta(x,0)$ is not vacant.
On the other hand, $\sigma_{0}$ is the first switching time of $x$ after
$a+T^{\bullet}$ but defined only if $\eta(x,a+T^{\bullet})$ is vacant.
  Whenever we have an event function ${g}(\alpha,W,\eta)$ in whose definition
$\sigma_{2}$ occurs, this function is always understood to have value 0 if
$\sigma_{2}$ is not defined (similarly with $\sigma_{0}$).
<!-- end definition-96 -->
<!-- definition-97: body_md -->
\label{def:rectangles}[Rectangles used in the computation property]
                                                                        
  Let 
 \gloprocw.cap@\( W_{0}(x, a), W_{1}(x, a) \).))) 
 \begin{align*}
       I_{0}(x)    &= \left[x-0.1{B} ,x+1.1{B} \right), \quad I_{1}(x) = \left[x-2.1{B} ,x+3.1{B} \right), 
\\   W_{j}(x,a) &= I_{j}(x)\times(a-2T^{\bullet},a+3T^{\bullet}] \quad (j=0,1),
   \\   {f}_{j}(x,a,\eta) &= \text{the event function for }
    \mathopen\{\mskip 1mu\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Damage\/}}}(\eta)\cap W_{j}(x,a) = \emptyset\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} \quad (j=0,1).
 \end{align*}
<!-- end definition-97 -->
<!-- definition-98: body_md -->
\label{def:affecting}
We will say that damage \emph{affects} cell \( (x,t) \) \emph{directly}, if it
intersects with  \( I_{0}(x) \) at time \( t \), with \( I_{j}(x) \)
as in Definition~\ref{def:rectangles}.
It affects a cell \emph{via neighbors}, if it  intersects \( I_{1}(x) \).
<!-- end definition-98 -->
<!-- condition-6: body_md -->
\label{cond:comput}
  This property consists of several condition types.
For each type \( \alpha \) used here except \( \alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{rand\/}}},j) \), we 
have \(  b(\alpha)=0 \), that is the corresponding events \( {g}(\alpha(\cdot),W,\eta) \) are
simply prohibited in the trajectory.
  On the other hand,
 \[
   b(\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{rand\/}}},j))=0.5+\varepsilon'\quad (j=0,1).
 \]
  \begin{cjenum}

 \item\label{i:comput.rand}
  Coin-tossing, for \( j=0,1 \):
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\alpha(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{rand\/}}},j),\;W_{0}(x,a),\;\eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)} = {f}_{0}(x,a,\eta)
 \{\cmexists\sigma_{2}\land \eta(x,\sigma_{2}).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Rand\/}}}}=j\}.
 \]

  \item\label{i:comput.dwell-pd-bd}
  The length of dwell periods must be between \( {T_{\bullet}} \) and \( T^{\bullet} \):
 \[
 {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{dw-p-bd\/}}},\; W_{0}(x,a),\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)} = {f}_{0}(x,a,\eta)
  {h}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{dw-p-bd\/}}},x,a,\eta)
 \]
  where \( {h}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{dw-p-bd\/}}},x,a)=1 \) if \( \eta \) has a dwell period shorter than
\( {T_{\bullet}} \) in \( W_{0}(x,a) \) or has a dwell period longer than \( T^{\bullet} \) there
(and, as always, 0 otherwise).

 \item\label{i:comput.legal-comp}
  Whenever \( W_{0}(x,a) \) is damage-free, the transition at
\( \sigma_{2} \) is a legal one:
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{legal-comp\/}}},\; W_{0}(x,a),\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)} 
 = {f}_{0}(x, a, \eta)
    \{ \cmexists\sigma_{2}\land\neg\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{legal\/}}}(\eta(x,\sigma_{2}-), \eta(x,\sigma_{2})\}.
 \]

 \item\label{i:comput.legal-birth}
   Whenever \( W_{1}(x,a) \) is damage-free and \( \sigma_{0} \) exists,
\( x \) either has a creator or is emerging (see Definition~\ref{def:creator-emerging}).
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{newborn\/}}},\; W_{1}(x,a),\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)} = {f}_{1}(x, a, \eta)
 \{\cmexists\sigma_{0}\land\neg{h}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{newborn\/}}}, x, a, \eta) \}
 \]
 where \( {h}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{newborn\/}}}, x, a, \eta)=1 \) if \( x \) has a creator for time 
\( \sigma_{0} \), or \( \eta(x,\sigma_{0}) \) is emerging.
Also, the transition in \( \sigma_{0} \) is a legal one:
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{legal-birth\/}}},\; W_{0}(x,a),\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)} = {f}_{0}(x, a, \eta)
    \{\cmexists\sigma_{0}\land\neg\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{legal\/}}}(\eta(x,\sigma_{0}-), \eta(x,\sigma_{0}))\}.
 \]

 \item\label{i:comput.trans}
  Whenever \( W_{1}(x,a) \) is damage-free, the transition
  function applies, based on observation at some
  (unspecified) time point during the \emph{observation interval} (``atomicity'')\index{atomicity}:
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{trans\/}}},\; W_{1}(x,a),\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)} = {f}_{1}(x, a, \eta)
  \{\cmexists\sigma_{2}\land\neg{h}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{trans\/}}}, x, a, \eta)\}
 \]
 where \( {h}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{trans\/}}}, x, a, \eta)=1 \) if there is a
 \( t'\in (\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}-{T_{\bullet}}/4] \) with
 \[
    \eta(x,\sigma_{2}).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}} = \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}(\eta,x,t').\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}}.
 \]

  \item \label{i:comput.creation}
  A cell cannot stay vacant if it has would-be creators for a
long time and has no neighbor potentially blocking the creation:
 \[
   {g}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{no-birth\/}}},\; W_{1}(x,a),\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)} = {f}_{1}(x, a, \eta)
 {h}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{no-birth\/}}}, x, a, \eta)
 \]
  where \( {h}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{no-birth\/}}}, x, a, \eta)=1 \) if the following conditions hold:
   \begin{romanenum}
    \item \( \eta(x,t) \) is vacant for all \( t\in[a,a+3T^{\bullet}] \);
    \item for each \( t\in [a,a+2T^{\bullet}] \) there is a
\( j\in\{-1,1\} \) such that \( (j,\vartheta_{j}(x,t)) \) is a potential creator of some
(non-vacant) state;
\item\label{i:obstacle-c}
  there is no non-vacant \( \eta(y,t) \) with \( 0<|y-x|<{B}  \), \( t\in[a,a+3T^{\bullet}] \).
   \end{romanenum}
  \end{cjenum}
<!-- end condition-6 -->
<!-- example-21: body_md -->
To obtain a deterministic cellular automaton
as a special case of robust media,
set \( {T_{\bullet}}=T^{\bullet} \), \( r=1 \), \( \varepsilon=0 \), require
that the histories have empty damage and that the
transition function not give a vacant value.

\begin{sloppypar}
The connection between primitive variable-period media and robust
media will be set up via a trivial simulation.
Let \( M_{1}=-var({\mathbb{S}}_{1}, {\Lambda}, \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1},{B} ,{T_{\bullet}},T^{\bullet},\varepsilon) \).
We make the additional assumptions that
the transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1} \)                    
satisfies the time marking Condition~\ref{cond:time-mark}.
We define a simple simulation \( \Phi^{*} \) by this medium of the robust
medium
 \[
  M_{2}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Rob\/}}}({\mathbb{S}}_{2}, {\Lambda}, \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2}, {B} , {T_{\bullet}}, T^{\bullet}, \varepsilon, \varepsilon, 1).
 \]
Set \( {\mathbb{S}}_{2} = {\mathbb{S}}_{1}\times \{0,1\} \), 
identify \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1} \) with \( {\mathbb{S}}_{1}\times\{0\} \), and denoting
\( {\mathbb{S}}'_{1}={\mathbb{S}}_{1}\times\{1\} \), let
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vacant\/}}}_{2}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vacant\/}}}_{1}\cup{\mathbb{S}}'_{1} \),
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Bad\/}}}_{2}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Bad\/}}}_{1}\cup{\mathbb{S}}'_{1} \).
Thus, some new bad states are introduced by turning on a new bit which we
can call the ``bad bit''.
The transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{2} \) is essentially the same as
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{1} \): it ignores the bad bit. 
It also satisfies Condition~\ref{cond:cling} 
trivially: it never destroys or creates cells.  
\end{sloppypar}

Let \( g_{1} \) be the event function used in the definition of medium \( M_{1} \).
We give the definition of \( s=\eta^{*}(x,t)=\Phi^{*}(\eta)(x,t) \) for each
\( \eta \).
If \( x \) is not an integer multiple of \( {B}  \) then \( s=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \).
If \( {g}_{1}{\bigl(\mskip 1mu\alpha,\; \{x\}\times(t',t],\; \eta\mskip 1mu\bigr)}=1 \) for some \( t'<t \)
and some \( \alpha\ne\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{coin\/}}} \) then \( s=(\eta(x,t),1) \) (as some condition is violated, the
bad bit is turned on), else \( s=(\eta(x,t),0) \).

It can be verified that this is indeed a simulation.
<!-- end example-21 -->
<!-- notation-9: body_md -->
\label{n:det-subfield}
Only field $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}}$ will be subdivided into subfields: therefore subfields
$\eta.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Det\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}$ will be denoted simply as $\eta.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}$, without danger of
confusion.
<!-- end notation-9 -->
<!-- definition-99: body_md -->
\label{def:amp-complex}
Consider an amplifier \( (M_{k},\Phi_{k}) \) where \( \Phi_{k}=(\varphi_{k*},\Phi^{*}_{k}) \).
For a sequence of fields \( (\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}}_{k}) \) and parameters \( D_{k},\varepsilon''_{k}\),
our amplifiers will use a code complex
  \begin{align*}
   \mathbf{H} = (\varphi_{k},\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}}_{k}, \gamma_{k})_{k\ge 1}
  \end{align*}
as in~\eqref{eq:H},
and they will have in addition the trickle-down property as in Definition~\ref{def:amp-trickle}
for the fields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}_{k}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}}_{k} \).
We will call such an amplifier an \emph{amplifier complex}.
<!-- end definition-99 -->
<!-- condition-7: body_md -->
\label{cond:Payload-invar-hist}
We require  transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Pl-trans\/}}}_{1} \) to be commutative in
the sense of Definition~\ref{def:commutative}.
<!-- end condition-7 -->
<!-- definition-100: body_md -->
\label{def:carries}
In a robust medium $M$, recall the transition function \( t=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{a}}) \)
from~\eqref{eq:rob-trans}. with input vector ${\mathbf{r}}=(r_{-1},r_{0},r_{1})$ and
the adjacency bits \( {\mathbf{a}}=(a_{-1},a_{1}) \).
We will say that it 
 \emph{carries}\index{transition function!carries} the payload transition
function $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Pl-trans\/}}}$\gloprocrd-trans@$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Pl-trans\/}}}$.))) if the condition
\( t\ne\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \), \( r_{0}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Germ\/}}}\),  \( {\mathbf{a}}=(1,1) \) implies
\( t.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}} = \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Pl-trans\/}}}({\mathbf{r}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}}) \).
<!-- end definition-100 -->
<!-- definition-101: body_md -->
The string $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{prog\/}}}$ will be called a
 \emph{uniform program (with complexity coefficient
$c$)}\index{program!uniform} for the functions $f_{k}$ if there is some
constant $c$ such that it computes on the universal computing medium
$\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Univ\/}}}$ the value $f_{k}({{\mathbf{r}}})$ from $k,{{\mathbf{r}}}$ with space- and
time-complexities bounded by $c(\log k + |{\mathbf{r}}|)$ where $|{\mathbf{r}}|$ is the total
number of bits in the arguments ${\mathbf{r}}$.
  If a sequence $(f_{k})$ of functions has a uniform program it is called
\emph{uniform}.
As a special case, a sequence of constants $c_{k}$ is uniform if it is
computable with space- and time complexities $c\log k$ from the index $k$.
<!-- end definition-101 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:frame-conds}
   The parameters satisfy the conditions above.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Conditions~\eqref{eq:cap-lbd-1}, \eqref{eq:bw-lb}, \eqref{eq:bw-b3} and~\eqref{eq:Ubd}
 are satisfied for large            
 \( R \).
 For inequality~\eqref{eq:cap-lbd-2}, assuming \( R>2 \),  note first that
 \begin{align*}
   \frac{\delta_{k+1}}{\delta_{k}}=\frac{{Q}_{k}w_{k}}{{Q}_{k+1}w_{k+1}}
   =\frac{(k+1)^{2}}{k^{2}R}.
\end{align*}
  \begin{align*}
                                                                  
                                                     
                                                       
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Cap\/}}}_{k+1}(1+\delta_{k+1})&={B}_{k+1}(1+\delta_{k+1})^{2}
    \\      &= {B}_{k+1}(1+\delta_{k+1}(2+\delta_{k+1}))
    \\       &= {B}_{k+1}(1+\delta_{k}\frac{(k+1)^{2}}{k^{2}R}.(2+\delta_{k+1}))
  \end{align*}
  The multiplier of \( \delta_{k} \) on the right-hand side is smaller than 1 for large \( R \).
Condition~\eqref{eq:bw-b2} reduces to 
\begin{align*}
  1+\delta_{k} &> (1 + \delta_{k+1})k^{2}/(k+1)^{2},
\end{align*}
which is true.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:amp}\index{lemma@Lemma!Amplifier}
  For large enough $R$ there is a uniform amplifier complex with the
  parameters introduced above, which also obeys the following conditions:
  \begin{cjenum}

  \item  Medium 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:M_{k}}
   M_{k}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Rob\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{k},{B}_{k},{T_{\bullet}}_{k},T^{\bullet}_{k},\varepsilon_{k},\varepsilon'_{k}).
 \end{equation}
 is robust.

  \item The damage map of the simulation $\Phi_{k}$ is given as in
Definition~\ref{def:damage-map}.

\item The function $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}_{k}$ carries the payload
  transition function $\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Pl-trans\/}}}_{k}$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:carries}.

\end{cjenum}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- definition-102: body_md -->
\label{def:info-field}
   Field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) consists of the subfields \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Pl-redun\/}}}} \),
   \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Util\/}}}} \) (referred to mostly as just \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Pl-redun\/}}}} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Util\/}}}} \)).
   \gloprocinfo.main@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}}, \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Pl-redun\/}}}}, \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}}.\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Util\/}}}} \).)))
The track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}} \) contains the intended original information,
The track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Pl-redun\/}}}} \) contains ``error check bits'' for the track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Payload\/}}}} \)
as in Example~\ref{xmp:err-corr-code},
while the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Util\/}}}} \) track contains other parts of the represented information of the
simulated colony (along with its own error checks).
<!-- end definition-102 -->
<!-- definition-103: body_md -->
\label{def:adjacency}
Recall the transition function \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Tr\/}}}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{a}}) \) where \( {\mathbf{a}}=(a_{-1},a_{1}) \) says
whether the left and right neighbor is adjacent.
In our rule language we will refer to \( a_{j} \) as 
\begin{align*}
 \ensuremath{\mathord{\textrm{adj-nb}}}(j) .
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-103 -->
<!-- definition-104: body_md -->
\label{def:colonies}
The values of the address field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}} \) will vary in \( \left[-{Q} ,2{Q} \right) \).
The \emph{colony} of a cell \( x \) is the set \( C=\mathopen\{\verythinmathskipz+i{B} : i\in\left[0,{Q}\right)\mskip 1mu\mathclose\} \)
whose starting cell is \( z = x-(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}(x) \bmod {Q} ) {B}  \).
We will also say that \( x \) \emph{belongs} to colony \( C \).
The \emph{originating colony} of a cell \( x \)
is the colony \( D \) whose starting cell is \( x-\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}(x) {B}  \).
We will also say that \( x \) \emph{originates} at colony \( D \).
The cells whose colony is their originating colony, will be called
\emph{inner cells}\index{cell!inner}, the other ones will be called
\emph{outer cells}\index{cell!outer}.
Two neighbor cells will be called \emph{space-consistent} if they originate at the same colony.
<!-- end definition-104 -->
<!-- definition-105: body_md -->
\label{def:cell-kinds}
Cells will be of a few different \emph{kinds}\index{cell!kind}, distinguished by
the field 
 \gloprockind@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}} \).))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}.
\]
The possible kinds are listed in~\eqref{eq:strength} below.
 \gloproclatent@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Latent\/}}} \).))) \gloprocgerm@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Germ\/}}} \).)))\gloprocchannel@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Channel\/}}} \).)))\gloprocgrowth@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Growth\/}}} \).)))
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Member\/}}} \)\gloprocmember@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Member\/}}} \).))) 
 \index{cell!vacant} 
 \index{cell!latent} 
 \index{cell!germ} 
 \index{cell!channel} 
 \index{cell!growth} 
 \index{cell!member} 
The kind of non-latent, non-germ, cells is determined by \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}} \).
Since it will be possible to determine from the age of a cell whether it
has kind \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Channel\/}}} \) or \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Growth\/}}} \),
We will sometimes use therefore just one value 
 \gloprocext@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Ext\/}}}_{j} \).))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Ext\/}}}_{j}
 \]
in place of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Growth\/}}}_{j} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Channel\/}}}_{j} \).
The kinds of cells are ordered by a property called \emph{strength} 
\index{cell!strength}
as follows:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:strength}
\begin{aligned}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} &< \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Latent\/}}} < \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Germ\/}}} < \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Channel\/}}}_{-1}<\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Channel\/}}}_{1}
\\       & < \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Growth\/}}}_{-1} < \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Growth\/}}}_{1} < \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Member\/}}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
 If a cell needs to be created, overlapping in body a another one then if the
 new cell is stronger, the weaker one will be erased.
 This is the only way a cell can turn vacant see the later
 Condition~\ref{cond:cling} (Cling-to-Life).
Let us discuss each kind.
 \begin{itemize}
  \item
The relation \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}(x,t)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vac\/}}} \) means that there is no cell at
site \( x \) at time \( t \).
  \item
A cell will be called \emph{dead}\index{cell!dead} if it is vacant or
latent, and \emph{live}\index{cell!live} otherwise.
\emph{Killing}\index{killing} a cell \( x \) means turning it latent. 
\emph{Erasing}\index{erasing} it means turning it vacant. 

  \item The \emph{member} cells are ``inner'' cells as defined above;
they are the strongest kind in order to maintain the integrity of colonies.

  \item Cells of kind \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Ext\/}}}_{j} \) are outer cells.
A \emph{right outer} cell has addresses \( \ge {Q}  \), and a \emph{left
outer} cell has addresses \( <0 \).

  \item Left channel cells are weaker than right channel cells which are weaker than growth cells.
This way, a right-growing channel will erase the left-growing
one if it is in its way, and information need not be transmitted between two channels.
Also, left channel cells can grow only until address \( -{Q} +1 \), and right ones
only until \( 2{Q} -2 \): thus a channel cannot be extended to cover a full colony.

\item \emph{Germ} cells exist at the highest level of the hierarchy, in the sense that
  they are not part of any colony simulating some higher-level cell.
  They also have the function to carry out a computation, the \emph{payload}
  of the whole construction.
The member cells on lower levels will receive the results of this computation by a
feature of the simulation called \emph{trickle-down}.
Germ cells have addresses in \( \left[-2{Q} ,3{Q} \right) \).
                                                              
 \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-105 -->
<!-- condition-8: body_md -->
\label{cond:vac-to-lat}
 \index{condition@Condition!Latent Cells}
  A vacant cell can only turn into a latent one.
<!-- end condition-8 -->
<!-- condition-9: body_md -->
\label{cond:outer-info}
Suppose that \( \varphi^{*}(\eta)(x,t)\notin\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Bad\/}}} \), the colony with base \( x \)
at time \( t \) is full and is covered with member cells belonging to the same
work period, and is not affected by damage (as in Definition~\ref{def:affecting}).                      
Then \( \varphi^{*}(\eta)(x,t) \) depends only on the \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) track of this
colony via some decoding function \( \alpha^{*} \).
If the colony is covered with germ or outer cells then the state
decoded from this track is latent.
<!-- end condition-9 -->
<!-- definition-106: body_md -->
\label{def:expansion-period}
The interval before age \( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{compute-start}}}} \) is called the \emph{retrieval period}: then
the colony retrieves information from neighbor colonies.
The constant \( K \) will make it substantially longer than the
transition period \( (\ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{grow-start}}}},{U}] \) at the end of the work period when the information to be
sent to neighbor colonies would change.
The age intervals \( (0,\ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{compute-start}}}}] \) and 
\( (\ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{grow-start}}}},\ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{grow-end}}}}] \) for non-germ outer cells
and \( (0,\ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{grow-end}}}}] \) for germ cells   
will be called \emph{expansion periods}.
\index{period!expansion}\index{cell!expansion}
Cells in their expansion period are called \emph{expansion cells}.
<!-- end definition-106 -->
<!-- definition-107: body_md -->
\label{def:cut}
  The application of the rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Finish\/}}}} \) will also be called a \emph{cut}.
<!-- end definition-107 -->
<!-- condition-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:dooming}\index{condition@Condition!Dooming}
Only the following rules can change the field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Doomed\/}}}} \) without killing the cell:
 \begin{djenum}

  \item The sub-rules \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Adapt\/}}}} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Heal\/}}}} \) (defined later) can
create doomed or non-doomed cells.

  \item At \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}=\ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{proc-payload-start}}}} \), we possibly doom each cell.

 \end{djenum}
<!-- end condition-10 -->
<!-- definition-108: body_md -->
\label{def:timing}
  Recall the definition of \( \lambda \) in~\eqref{eq:lg-less-2}.
We introduce some delay constants \( {p}_{0} < {p}_{1} < {p}_{2} < {p}_{3} \)
 \gloprocp@\( {p}_{i} \).)))
  whose value will be defined below, further \gloprocthm:greek@\( \tau_{i} \).)))
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:tau_{i}}
  \tau_{i}  = ({p}_{i}+1)T^{\bullet}.
 \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-108 -->
<!-- definition-109: body_md -->
\label{def:loc-maint}
Certain fields, called
\emph{locally maintained}\index{field!locally maintained}, will be
kept constant over the colony, for most of the work period.
Each such field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) has a \emph{default value}.
The updating will of such a field always happen at a specific age
called the \emph{update age}\index{update!age}.
Let
\begin{align}\label{eq:n-loc-maint}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{n\/}}}_{\text{l-m}}
\end{align}
be the (constant) number of update ages for locally maintained fields.
A cell's locally maintained field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) is said to be 
\emph{stable}\index{stable} if its age is at distance \( \ge \Delta \) from the
update age, where this constant is defined below in~\eqref{eq:split-n}.
An age \( n \) is called \emph{stable} for \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) if \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) is stable at age \( n \).
It is called simply \emph{stable} if it is stable for all locally maintained fields,
and is also at distance \( \ge \Delta \) from ages 0,
\( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{compute-start}}}} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{grow-end}}}} \).
<!-- end definition-109 -->
<!-- example-22: body_md -->
\label{xmp:loc-maint}
Here are some examples of locally maintained fields.
 \begin{itemize}

   \item The Boolean track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Doomed\/}}}} \)\gloprocdoomed@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Doomed\/}}}} \).))) will be set 
to 1 (true) if the represented big
cell must be removed (the site to become vacant), and 0 otherwise.
Its default value is 0 (false).
Its update age is \( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{proc-payload-start}}}} \) (defined in~\eqref{eq:compute-start}).
Cells with \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Doomed\/}}}}=1 \) are called \emph{doomed}\index{cell!doomed}.

  \item The track 
 \gloprocgrowing@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Growing\/}}}}_{j} \).))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Growing\/}}}}_{j}\in\{0,1\},\; j\in\{-1,1\}
\]
signifies the collective decision of the colony to
grow a new neighbor colony in direction \( j \).
Its update age is \( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{proc-payload-start}}}} \).
The field \gloproccreating@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{j} \).))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{j}\in\{0,1\},\; j\in\{-1,1\}
\]
will be used to control the creation of a new neighbor.
Its default value, in a vacant or new latent cell, is 0.
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{j}=1 \) makes a cell a potential creator in direction \( j \)
in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:creator-emerging}.
The value of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{j} \) of a big cell will be broadcast into the
locally maintained track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Growing\/}}}}_{j} \) of the cells of its representing colony.
\item The track \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Pl-commands\/}}}} \) will contain commands for the processing
  of payload: see Section~\ref{sec:comp}.
 \end{itemize}
<!-- end example-22 -->
<!-- condition-11: body_md -->
\label{cond:loc-maint}
Age 0 is an update age for all locally maintained fields other than \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Doomed\/}}}} \).
If \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Doomed\/}}}}=1 \) then \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Growing\/}}}}_{j}=0 \) for \( j\in\{-1,1\} \).
<!-- end condition-11 -->
<!-- definition-110: body_md -->
\label{def:fit}
   Two neighbor cells \( x<y \) with colors \( c,d \) will be expected to have \emph{fitting} colors.
   This is expressed by the relation \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Fit\/}}}_{1}(c,d) \) which is 1 if the colors fit and 0 otherwise.
   Let
   \begin{align*}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Fit\/}}}_{-1}(c,d)=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Fit\/}}}_{1}(d,c).
\end{align*}
We will use two examples of the fitting relation:
\begin{djenum}
  \item\label{i:fit.sorg}
 A color can be an arbitrary symbol from a finite alphabet, and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Fit\/}}}_{j}(c,d)=1 \)
 if and only if \( c=d \).
\item\label{i:fit.comp}
  A color is an element of \( \{-1,0,1\} \), and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Fit\/}}}_{1}(c,d)=1 \) if \( c\le d\le c+1 \).
In what follows we concentrate on the second case, as the other case is treated analogously, only
simpler.
The function of color is in this case is the following: the area of space where payload computation is happening is marked by  color 0, while the space to its left and right by
colors \( -1 \) and \( 1 \) respectively.
\end{djenum}
<!-- end definition-110 -->
<!-- definition-111: body_md -->
\label{def:time-consistency}
Two cells \( x \) and \( y=x\pm {B}  \) with \( |\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}(x)-{\lfloor {Q} /2\rfloor}|<|\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}(y)-{\lfloor {Q} /2\rfloor}| \)
belong to the \emph{same work period}\index{period!work} if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:same-work-period}
  0 \le \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}(x)-\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}(y) \le 1.  
\end{equation}
They \emph{straddle a work period boundary}
\index{period!work!boundary} if \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}(x)=0 \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}(y)={U} -1 \).
If one of these cases holds then we will say they are \emph{time-consistent}.
<!-- end definition-111 -->
<!-- definition-112: body_md -->
\label{def:siblings}
Two cells \( x,x+j{B}  \) for \( j\in\{-1,1\} \)
are \emph{siblings}\index{sibling} if
                                                         
one of the following properties holds. 
 \begin{djenum}

   \item  They belong to the same work period, originate at the same colony
(see the definition of originating colony at the beginning of
Section~\ref{sec:cell-kinds}), either both are germ cells or neither of them is.
                                                                             
If \( x \) is a colony cell and \( x+j{B}  \) is a growth cell then \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Growing\/}}}}_{j}(x)=1 \) is
also required.

  \item They belong to the same colony (see the definition of the colony
of a cell at the beginning of Section~\ref{sec:cell-kinds}), 
and straddle a work period boundary.

\item They have fitting colors.

\item If they are germ cells with \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{G-growing\/}}}(\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}}) \) then
  they agree in their \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{G-size\/}}}} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dominant\/}}}} \) fields
  (see Section~\ref{sec:germ-growth}).
\end{djenum}
<!-- end definition-112 -->
<!-- definition-113: body_md -->
\label{def:domain}
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:maxDepth}
 \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{max-depth}}}} = \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{heal-span}}}}    
  \end{equation}
with value defined in~\eqref{eq:heal-span}.
An interval of cells in which the adjacent cells are siblings will be
called a \emph{domain}\index{domain}.
A domain of size \( n \) will also be called a
\emph{\( n \)-support}\index{support@support!\( n \)-} of its members.
For integer \( k>0 \), let us call two cells \( x,x+k{B}  \)
\emph{relatives}\index{relatives} if we can change the states of cells
\( x+j{B}  \) for \( j=1,\dots,k-1 \) in such a way that the cells
\( x,x+{B} ,\dots,x+k{B}  \) become a domain.
A colony with starting cell \( x \) will be called
\emph{full}\index{colony!full} if it is covered by a domain in such a way
that \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}(x+i{B} )\equiv i\pmod {Q}  \).
<!-- end definition-113 -->
<!-- definition-114: body_md -->
Let us call the \emph{left depth} of a cell \( x \) the size of the
largest domain of the form \( \{x-i {B} , x-(i-1){B} ,\dots,x\} \)
within a single colony containing \( x \).
The right depth is defined similarly.
For example, \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{depth\/}}}_{-1}(x)>1 \) \gloprocdepth@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{depth\/}}} \).)))
just means that \( x \) has a left sibling.

For a locally maintained field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \) we define the \emph{left depth}
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{depth\/}}}_{j,\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}}(x) \) \emph{for \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \)} of a cell \( x \) the size of the
largest interval of the form \( \{x-i {B} , x-(i-1){B} ,\dots,x\} \)
within a single colony containing \( x \) and having constant value of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}} \).

A cell will always try to keep track of its depths, up to the maximum
possible value.
It will use the fields \gloprocDepth@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Depth\/}}}} \).)))
 \begin{align*}
   \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Depth\/}}}}_{j}, \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Depth\/}}}}_{j,\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{F\/}}}}}
   \in\{1,\dots, \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{max-depth}}}}\},\  j\in\{-1,1\}.
 \end{align*}
 So if for example left depth is larger than \( \ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{max-depth}}}} \) then the cell may
 only see \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Depth\/}}}}_{-1}=\ensuremath{\mathinner{\textsf{\upshape{max-depth}}}} \).
<!-- end definition-114 -->
<!-- definition-115: body_md -->
\label{def:frozen}
There is 
             
                                             
                        
                                                            
      
a field  
 \gloprocfrozen@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Frozen\/}}}} \).)))\index{cell!frozen} 
 \begin{align*}
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Frozen\/}}}}\in[-\Delta,\Delta] \cap\mathbb{Z}
                                                                   
 \end{align*}
with the property that when \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Frozen\/}}}}\ne 0 \) then \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \) will not be
changed.
A cell with \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Frozen\/}}}}\ne 0 \) is called \emph{frozen}.
<!-- end definition-115 -->
<!-- condition-12: body_md -->
\label{cond:addr-age}
 \index{condition@Condition!Address and Age}
 \begin{cjenum}

  \item
  Only \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Finish\/}}}} \) can change \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}} \) of a live cell.

  \item
  Only \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{March\/}}}} \), \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Heal-sync\/}}}} \)
and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Finish\/}}}} \) can change \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Age\/}}}} \) of a live cell.
Of these, \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Heal-sync\/}}}} \) can do it when the cell is frozen and
the others when it is not.
 \end{cjenum}
<!-- end condition-12 -->
<!-- definition-116: body_md -->
\label{def:edges}
Suppose that cell \( x \) has no siblings in direction \( j \), that is it has
\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{depth\/}}}_{j}(x)=1 \).
It will be called a \emph{protected edge}\index{edge!protected} in that
direction if it is some legitimate boundary in that direction, in the sense
described below; otherwise, it will be
called an \emph{exposed edge}\index{edge!exposed}.
Recall expansion periods and cells in Definition~\ref{def:expansion-period}.
Essentially, growth edges are protected during the expansion period or
if the growth reached a colony end.
Here is a list of the types of protected edges, for non-germ cells.
For germ cells, the definition will be given in Section~\ref{sec:germ-growth}.
  \begin{description}

   \item[Member] Colony end-cell towards \( j \).

   \item[Expansion cell]
     During the expansion period, while \( j \) is the direction of expansion.
     After the expansion period,
     if the cell is a growth cell and a colony end-cell towards \( j \).
                                                                                    
                                           
                                                                                                
                                                      
     
                               
                                                                                
                                                           
                                       
                             

    \end{description}
In a rule, the condition  \gloprocxposed@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Xposed\/}}}_{j} \).))) 
    \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Xposed\/}}}_{j}.
 \]
 means that the cell \( {\mathbf{x}} \) applying the rule is an exposed edge in direction \( j \).
<!-- end definition-116 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:expose}
If a left exposed edge dies and its right sibling was not a
colony endcell, then this neighbor becomes a left exposed edge.
The same holds if we replace left with right.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The one case when this is not obvious is when the exposed edge is a left outer cell
past its expansion period but its neighbor may not be.
But the address-dependent nature of expansion periods as introduced
in Definition~\ref{def:expansion-period} forces then
the right sibling also to be past its expansion period.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- definition-117: body_md -->
\label{def:multi-domain}
A \emph{multi-domain}\index{domain!multi-} is one of the following kinds of set:
\begin{djenum}
  \item A domain.
  \item The union of some adjacent domains meeting in protected colony end-cells.
                    
                                                                             
                                                                         
                                 
\end{djenum}
<!-- end definition-117 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:short-exposed}
  If some maximal multi-domain has size \( <{Q} \), then the following holds:
  \begin{cjenum}
    \item One of its edges is exposed, with the following 
      exception: it consists of germ cells in their expansion period,
      contains a cell with address \( {Q}/2 \), and the
size is either \( >3 \), or 3; in the latter case
the adjacent neighbor cells of the domain are not live.
                             
  \item
If the size is \( \le {Q}-d \) with \( d>0 \), then at least one the exposed edges
cannot become protected by the death of an outside neighbor, or 
by shrinking, or by growing by fewer than \( d \) steps.
The only exception is a germ of size 3 of the above kind: it
may become protected if a neighbor dies.
  \end{cjenum}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- definition-118: body_md -->
We will have some one-bit fields
 \gloprocdying@\( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dying\/}}}} \).))) 
 \[
  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dying\/}}}}_{j}, \ j\in\{-1,0,1\},
 \]
with default value 0.
We will say that a cell \( x \) is \emph{dying} if \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dying\/}}}}_{0}(x)=1 \).
<!-- end definition-118 -->
<!-- condition-13: body_md -->
\label{cond:birth}
 \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Create\/}}}} \) and \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Birth\/}}}} \) are the only rules applicable to a vacant cell.
<!-- end condition-13 -->
<!-- notation-10: body_md -->
For a relation \( R \), let 
 \gloproc"<@\( a\stackrel{\scriptstyle R}{<} b \).))) 
 \[
  a\stackrel{\scriptstyle R}{<} b
 \]
  mean ``\( a<b \) or (\( a=b \) and \( R \) holds)''.
<!-- end notation-10 -->
<!-- definition-119: body_md -->
\label{def:Kind_j}
  Let \( j\in\{-1,1\} \).
 The field \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}_{j} \) shows the kind of the cell intended to be created
  in the adjacent neighbor in direction \( j \).
  Let
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:NonGermLess}
  \begin{aligned}
    \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Non-germ-less\/}}}_{j}&\mathrel{\;\Leftrightarrow\;} Kind_{-j}^{j}\stackrel{\scriptstyle j=1}{>}\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}
     \land \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Depth\/}}}}_{j}^{j}>1  \land  \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dying\/}}}}^{j}_{j}=0
    \\ &\land (\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}^{-j}=\ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Vacant\/}}}\lor \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}_{-j}^{j}\stackrel{\scriptstyle j=1}{>}\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}_{j}^{-j}).   
\end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-119 -->
<!-- definition-120: body_md -->
\label{def:parent}
If a latent cell \( x \) came to life by the rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Adapt\/}}}}(j) \)
then we will say that it has been \emph{animated}.  
The neighbor in direction \( j \) will be called its \emph{parent}\index{cell!parent}.
(The latent cell could have been created earlier by a neighbor, 
which we could call a ``creating parent''.)
In case the same result could also have arisen using the neighbor on the
other side then the parent cell is defined as
the one closer to the center of its colony (or to the left if the animated cell
is the center).
<!-- end definition-120 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
Suppose that
 \begin{cjenum}

  \item A cell \( x \) has just been adapted at time \( t \) to a non-germ
neighbor \( y=\vartheta_{j}(x) \) (this rule being a
possible explanation for its becoming live);

  \item Rectangle 
                                                            
\( (x+\left[-2.1{B} ,3.1{B} \right))\times(t+ (-3T^{\bullet},0]) \) 
is damage-free;

  \item There is no colony-boundary between \( y \) and its sibling required
by the rule.

 \end{cjenum}
Then \( x \) and \( y \) stay siblings until after \( t \).
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The adaptation \( y \) to be non-dying.
Due to the minimum delay \( {p}_{0} \) in dying which they did not even
begin, these cells remain live till after \( t \).
Since there is no colony boundary between them, a cut (as in Definition~\ref{def:cut})
will not break the sibling relation of these cells either.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:creation}\index{lemma@Lemma!Creation}
Assume the following, with \( J=(t_{0},t_{0} + \tau_{0} + 11T^{\bullet}] \):
 \begin{cjenum}
  \item Rectangle 
\( \left[x-4.1{B} ,x+3.1{B} \right)\times J \) 
is damage-free;
  \item We have \( \eta(x-{B} ,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dying\/}}}}_{0}=\eta(x-{B} ,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Dying\/}}}}_{-1}=0 \), and
 \[
 \eta(x-{B} ,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}_{1} \ge \eta(y,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}\vee \eta(y,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Kind\/}}}}_{-1}
 \]
  for all live cells \( (y,t) \) in the rectangle \( \left[x,x+2{B} \right)\times J \).
 \end{cjenum}
Then \( \eta(x,t) \) is non-vacant for some \( t \) in \( J \).
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Assume, on the contrary, that \( x \) is vacant during all of \( J \), and
we will arrive at a contradiction.
The conditions imply that noise does not affect cell \( x-{B}  \), so it can obey its transition rule.
Hence part~\eqref{alg:create.vacant} of the rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Create\/}}}} \) sets 
\( \eta(x-{B} ,t).\ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{1}=1 \) at some \( t_{1}\le t_{0}+2T^{\bullet} \), and this
stays so while \( x \) is vacant.
                                                           
Condition~\ref{cond:comput}\ref{i:comput.creation} requires \( x \) to
become a cell by time \( t_{1}+2T^{\bullet} \) unless the body of some
cell overlaps the body of \( x \).
Suppose therefore that cell \( y \) overlaps the body of \( x \) before time
\( t_{2} = t_{1}+2T^{\bullet}\le t_{0}+4T^{\bullet} \).
Then \( y>x \), since in case \( y<x \),  cell \( y \) would overlap cell
\( x-{B}  \), which is assumed to be there during all this time interval.
This \( y \) disappears by time \( t_{3}=t_{2}+\tau_{0}+T^{\bullet}=t_{1}+\tau_{0}+5T^{\bullet} \).
Indeed, part~\eqref{alg:adapt.kill} of \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Adapt\/}}}} \) makes \( y \) latent within
\( \tau_{0} \), then part~\eqref{alg:adapt.sacrif} erases \( y \) within \( T^{\bullet} \).

If no similar obstacle cell \( y' \) arises before time
\( t_{4}=t_{3}+2T^{\bullet} = t_{1}+\tau_{0}+7T^{\bullet} \)
then again \( x \) would be created, so assume one appears.
This can only happen if \( y'+{B}  \) creates it (and hence is latent).
After it does, rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Create\/}}}} \) of Algorithm~\ref{alg:Create}
turns off \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{-1} \), turning which on again takes time \( \ge{p}_{0}{T_{\bullet}} \).
Now \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Adapt\/}}}} \) will erase \( y' \) by time
\( t_{5}=t_{4}+2T^{\bullet}= t_{0}+\tau_{0}+9T^{\bullet} \).
                                                        
                                                                 
                                                                              
No other
cell with \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{-1}=1 \) can arise by time \( t_{6}+2T^{\bullet}=t_{0}+\tau_{0}+11T^{\bullet} \);
partly for the same reason and partly because if \( y'+B \) is erased and a new latent cell
occupies its place then its \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Creating\/}}}}_{-1} \) is turned on only by a delay of \( {p}_{0}{T_{\bullet}} \),
as said in rule \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\texttt{\slshape{Create\/}}}} \) of Algorithm~\ref{alg:Create}.
As a result no new obstacle \( y'' \) can appear soon after \( y' \) has been erased.

Condition~\ref{cond:comput}\ref{i:comput.legal-birth}, allows only one other way for
a cell to appear, namely ``out of nothing''; but this
requires the cell to have no neighbors with a body within distance \( 2{B} \) of its body, and as
\( x-{B}  \) would be such a neighbor, this cannot happen.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- condition-14: body_md -->
\label{cond:growth-latent}
  If a cell has kind \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Growth\/}}} \) or \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textit{Germ\/}}} \) then its \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Info\/}}}} \) field's value is
  the symbol at \( \ensuremath{\mathord{\textsf{\slshape{Addr\/}}}}\bmod {Q} \) in the code of a latent big cell.
  (If, due to a fault, it does not have that value then this would be immediately corrected in the next step.)
<!-- end condition-14 -->
<!-- definition-121: body_md -->
Let
